nodes.statement: The proof of this theorem comprises a large portion of our work and breaks down into many sub-cases. Via a fiber sequence argument, it is equivalent to showing that Fr(M)/\!\!/ Diff(M) has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex, where Fr(M) is the frame bundle of M. In a similar vein to the proof of Theorem , we cut M up along embedded tori and prove the result for the simpler pieces, via a combination of the JSJ and geometric decompositions of our irreducible 3-manifold. We use this to reduce the proof to the case of hyperbolic manifolds, non-Haken Seifert-fibered manifolds, Haken Seifert-fibered manifolds, and Sol manifolds that are torus bundles over the circle. A schematic of the proof and its breakdown into cases is depicted in creffig:flowchartirreducible.

The proof of this theorem comprises a large portion of our work and breaks down into many sub-cases. Via a fiber sequence argument, it is equivalent to showing that $\mathrm{Fr}(M)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}(M)$ has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex, where $\mathrm{Fr}(M)$ is the frame bundle of $M$. In a similar vein to the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:more general Kontsevich-finiteness-conjecture}, we cut $M$ up along embedded tori and prove the result for the simpler pieces, via a combination of the JSJ  and geometric decompositions of our irreducible 3-manifold.

A schematic of the proof and its breakdown into cases is depicted in \cref{fig:flowchartirreducible}.

nodes.statement: Let X be a G-locally retractile space. [(1)] item Any G-equivariant map fcolon Y to X is a locally trivial fiber bundle. item If a G-equivariant map gcolon X to Z has local sections, then Z is also G-locally retractile. item If X is locally path connected, then X is also G_0-locally retractile for G_0 subset G the path component of the identity. item If G < H is a larger topological group such that the G-action on X extends to an H-action, then X is also H-locally retractile.
assumptions: Let X be a G-locally retractile space.
[(1)] item Any G-equivariant map fcolon Y to X is a locally trivial fiber bundle.
conclusions: item If a G-equivariant map gcolon X to Z has local sections, then Z is also G-locally retractile.
item If X is locally path connected, then X is also G_0-locally retractile for G_0 subset G the path component of the identity.
item If G < H is a larger topological group such that the G-action on X extends to an H-action, then X is also H-locally retractile.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem:locally-retractile}
    Let $X$ be a $G$-locally retractile space.
    \begin{enumerate}[(1)]
        \item 
        Any $G$-equivariant map $f\colon Y \to X$ is a locally trivial fiber bundle.
        \item 
        If a $G$-equivariant map $g\colon X \to Z$ has local sections, then $Z$ is also $G$-locally retractile.
        \item If $X$ is locally path connected, then $X$ is also $G_0$-locally retractile for $G_0 \subset G$ the path component of the identity.
        \item If $G < H$ is a larger topological group such that the $G$-action on $X$ extends to an $H$-action, then $X$ is also $H$-locally retractile.
    \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: The space of collars \[ Emb_partial M times \0\(partial M times I, M) = \ i in Emb(partial M times [0,1], M) \;|\; i_|partial M times \0\ = id_partial M \ \] is weakly contractible. It follows that the subgroup inclusion \[ Diff_U(M) to Diff_partial U(M setminus interiorU) \] is a weak equivalence for any compact codimension 0 submanifold U subset interiorM.
conclusions: The space of collars \[ Emb_partial M times \0\(partial M times I, M) = \ i in Emb(partial M times [0,1], M) \;|\; i_|partial M times \0\ = id_partial M \ \] is weakly contractible.
It follows that the subgroup inclusion \[ Diff_U(M) to Diff_partial U(M setminus interiorU) \] is a weak equivalence for any compact codimension 0 submanifold U subset interiorM.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{thm:contractible-collars}
    The space of collars
    \[
        \mathrm{Emb}_{\partial M \times \{0\}}(\partial M \times I, M) = \{ i \in \mathrm{Emb}(\partial M \times [0,1], M) \;|\; i_{|\partial M \times \{0\}} = \mathrm{id}_{\partial M} \}
    \]
    is weakly contractible.
    It follows that the subgroup inclusion
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}_U(M) \to \mathrm{Diff}_{\partial U}(M \setminus \interior{U})
    \]
    is a weak equivalence
    for any compact codimension $0$ submanifold $U \subset \interior{M}$.

nodes.statement: First we prove that X is a principal G-space if and only if we can find a family of subsets \U_i subset X\_i in I such that the action maps U_i times G hookrightarrow X are open embeddings and jointly cover X. If pcolon X to X/G is a G-principal bundle, then there is an open covering \U_i'\_i in I of X/G such that there are equivariant homeomorphisms alpha_icolon U_i' times G cong p^-1(U_i') over U_i'. We can then set U_i = alpha_i(U_i' times \1\). Conversely, if we have \U_i subset X\_iin I, then U_i' := p(U_i) is open because it is the image of the open map U_i times G hookrightarrow X to X/G, and p will be trivial over these U_i'. Applying this to G to G/H we find \V_j subset G\_j in J such that V_j times H hookrightarrow G are open embeddings covering G. Now we can set W_i,j to be the image of the embedding U_i times V_j subset U_i times G hookrightarrow X and these will be such that \[ W_i,j times H cong U_i times V_j times H hookrightarrow U_i times G hookrightarrow X \] are open embeddings covering X. Therefore X to X/H is an H-principal bundle.

First we prove that $X$ is a principal $G$-space if and only if we can find a family of subsets $\{U_i \subset X\}_{i \in I}$ such that the action maps $U_i \times G \hookrightarrow X$ are open embeddings and jointly cover $X$.
    If $p\colon X \to X/G$ is a $G$-principal bundle, then there is an open covering $\{U_i'\}_{i \in I}$ of $X/G$ such that there are equivariant homeomorphisms $\alpha_i\colon U_i' \times G \cong p^{-1}(U_i')$ over $U_i'$. We can then set $U_i = \alpha_i(U_i' \times \{1\})$.
    Conversely, if we have $\{U_i \subset X\}_{i\in I}$, then $U_i' := p(U_i)$ is open because it is the image of the open map $U_i \times G \hookrightarrow X \to X/G$, and $p$ will be trivial over these $U_i'$.

    Applying this to $G \to G/H$ we find $\{V_j \subset G\}_{j \in J}$ such that $V_j \times H \hookrightarrow G$ are open embeddings covering $G$.
    Now we can set $W_{i,j}$ to be the image of the embedding $U_i \times V_j \subset U_i \times G \hookrightarrow X$ and these will be such that 
    \[
        W_{i,j} \times H \cong U_i \times V_j \times H
        \hookrightarrow U_i \times G \hookrightarrow X
    \]
    are open embeddings covering $X$.
    Therefore $X \to X/H$ is an $H$-principal bundle.

We can then set U_i = alpha_i(U_i' times \1\). nodes.statement: For each orbit the map G to X defined by acting on any point x in X is a quotient map, so since the action is transitive we can identify X with the left quotient Hsetminus G by the stabiliser group H = Stab_G(x). We now compute \[ X /\!\!/ G = ((H setminus G) times EG)/G cong H setminus ((G times EG)/G) cong H setminus EG \] Because H = Stab_G(x) < G is such that G to H setminus G is a principal H-bundle and EG to G setminus EG = BG is also a principal bundle, creflem:principal-bundle-subgroup says that EG to H setminus EG is a principal bundle. Hence we may define EH := EG such that X simeq H setminus EG = BH = BStab_G(x). The homotopy fiber sequence is obtained from X to X/\!\!/ G to BG by rewriting the middle term.

    \[
        X /\!\!/ G = ((H \setminus G) \times EG)/G
        \cong H \setminus ((G \times EG)/G)
        \cong H \setminus EG

nodes.statement: All of these properties are standard, but we recall them here for the convenience of the reader. The homotopy orbits functor is the composite of the functor (-) times EG and the functor (-)/G. In a convenient category of topological spaces the cartesian product preserves all colimits in each variable, and the second functor preserves colimits because colimits commute, hence () follows. For () we note that (-)times Y certainly commutes with the first functor and it also commutes with the second functor because (-) times Y preserves all colimits and hence in particular preserves taking orbits by G. Item () follows form the long exact sequence for the fiber sequences X to X /\!\!/ G to BG. Because we now know that (-)/\!\!/ G preserves weak equivalences, to show () it will suffice to prove that the functor preserves the standard construction of the homotopy pushout as \[ X cup^h_Y Z = X cup_Y (Y times [0,1]) cup_Y Z. \] This indeed is preserved because we already noted that (-)/\!\!/ G preserves pushouts and products with trivial G-spaces. Finally, for (), let X_bullet be semi-simplicial G-space. Then there is a homeomorphism \|X_bullet /\!\!/ G\| cong \|X_bullet\|/\!\!/ G because the fat geometric realisation is a colimit of products with the topological n-simplices, which are trivial G-spaces.

conclusions: Then E is homotopy finite.

nodes.statement: Without loss of generality B itself is a finite CW complex and p is a fibration. We proceed by induction on the dimension of B and the number of cells in B. If B is a disk, then E is equivalent to the homotopy fiber and the claim follows. Otherwise, we can find an open decomposition B = U cup V where U, V, and U cap V are all equivalent to finite CW complexes that have either fewer cells than B or a lower dimension. (Let, for instance, U subset B be an open cell, x in U and V = B setminus \x\.) By induction hypothesis, we see that p^-1(U), p^-1(V) and p^-1(U cap V) must all be equivalent to finite CW complexes, as they are fibrations over a homotopy finite space and have homotopy finite fibers. Now E = p^-1(U) cup_p^-1(U cap V) p^-1(V) is a homotopy pushout of homotopy finite spaces and as such it is homotopy finite as claimed.

nodes.statement: Let S(X, perp) denote the (discrete) simplicial complex where vertices are points in X and n+1 vertices span an n-simplex if and only if they are orthogonal. Let C(X, perp) denote the space of non-empty unordered orthogonal configurations, i.e.~the subspace of coprod_kge 0 X^k/Sym_k of those ulx = [x_1,dots,x_k] such that x_i perp x_j holds for all i neq j. We make C(X, perp) into a topological poset with respect to the subset ordering subseteq. For any orthogonal uly = (y_1,dots,y_n) we define S(X, perp)^perp uly subset S(X, perp) as the full subcomplex on those vertices x that are orthogonal to all y_i. Similarly, we define C(X, perp)^perp uly subset C(X,perp) as the topological subposet containing those configurations that are orthogonal to uly.

\label{defn - C/S(X, perp)}
    Let $S(X, \perp)$ denote the (discrete) simplicial complex where vertices are points in $X$ and $n+1$ vertices span an $n$-simplex if and only if they are orthogonal.
    Let $C(X, \perp)$ denote the space of non-empty unordered orthogonal configurations, 
    \emph{i.e.}~the subspace of $\coprod_{k\ge 0} X^k/\mathrm{Sym}_k$ of those $\ul{x} = [x_1,\dots,x_k]$ such that $x_i \perp x_j$ holds for all $i \neq j$.
    We make $C(X, \perp)$ into a topological poset with respect to the subset ordering $\subseteq$.
    For any orthogonal $\ul{y} = (y_1,\dots,y_n)$ we define $S(X, \perp)^{\perp \ul{y}} \subset S(X, \perp)$ as the full subcomplex on those vertices $x$ that are orthogonal to all $y_i$.
    Similarly, we define $C(X, \perp)^{\perp \ul{y}} \subset C(X,\perp)$ as the topological subposet containing those configurations that are orthogonal to $\ul{y}$.

nodes.statement: Write C := C(X, perp) and S := S(X, perp), and let C^delta be C equipped with the discrete topology. First, note that C is the poset of simplices of S and hence B(C^delta) = |N_bullet C^delta| is the barycentric subdivision of |S|. In particular they are homeomorphic, and similarly |N_bullet(C^perp uly)^delta| cong |S^perp uly|. From now on all geometric realisations are ``fat'', i.e.~we do not quotient by the relations imposed by the degeneracy maps. For simplicial sets the fat and thin geometric realisations are always equivalent . We define the following bisimplicial subspace of (N_bullet C)^delta times N_bullet C: \[ D_p,q := \ ((ulx^0 subseteq dots subseteq ulx^p),(uly^0 subseteq dots subseteq uly^q)) in N_p C^delta times N_q C \;|\; ulx^p perp uly^q \. \] Note that by ulx^p perp uly^q we mean that ulx^i perp uly^j for all i and j. We will also need the diagonal of D_bullet, bullet, which is the simplicial space given by (Delta D)_p := D_p,p. Consider the diagram \[ [row sep = small] && \|N_bullet C^delta\| ar[dd, "iota"] \\ \|(Delta D)_bullet\| ar[r, "alpha"', "simeq"] ar[rru, bend left] ar[rrd, bend right] & \|\| D_bullet, bullet \|\| ar[dr, "varepsilon"'] ar[ur, "gamma"] & \\ && \|N_bullet C\| \] where the map iota is the canonical map from the discretisation, gamma projects to the ulx^i and varepsilon projects to the uly^j. The map alpha is the inclusion of the diagonal and it is a weak equivalence by . Claim: The outside diagram commutes up to homotopy, i.e.~iota circ gamma circ alpha simeq varepsilon circ alpha. Proof of claim: Consider the topological subposet Q subset C^delta times C containing those tuples (ulx, uly) satsifying ulx perp uly. The nerve of Q is isomorphic to the diagonal Delta D: the homeomorphism N_p Q cong (Delta D)_p = D_p,p is given by the tautological map \[ ((ulx^0, uly^0) subseteq dots subseteq (ulx^p,uly^p)) longmapsto ((ulx^0 subseteq dots subseteq ulx^p), (uly^0 subseteq dots subseteq uly^p)). \] The two maps iota circ gamma circ alpha and varepsilon circ alpha are obtained as the realisation of the two poset-maps pr_1, pr_2: Q to C defined by pr_1(ulx, uly) := ulx and pr_2 (ulx, uly) := uly, respectively. We can also define a third map q:Q to C by q(ulx, uly) = ulx cup uly, which is well-defined since ulx perp uly in Q, and therefore it follows that ulx and uly are disjoint as subsets of X (perp is anti-reflexive). Now, since ulx subseteq (ulx cup uly) supseteq uly, Lemma implies that \[ iota circ gamma circ alpha = B(pr_1) simeq B(q) simeq B(pr_2) = varepsilon circ alpha, \] which proves the claim. For fixed q the projection map varepsilon_q: \|D_bullet,q\| to N_q C is a micro Serre fibration by . (To apply this proposition observe that N_q C^perp ulx subseteq N_q C is open.) The fiber varepsilon^-1(beta) of this at some beta = (uly^0 subseteq dots subseteq uly^q) in N_q C is isomorphic to the simplicial set N_bullet ( C^perp uly^q )^delta. The realisation of this is homeomorphic to B( (C^perp uly^q)^delta ) cong \|S^perp uly^q\|, which we assumed to be (n-1)-connected. Hence, by the map varepsilon_q: \|D_bullet,q\| to N_q C is n-connected. Moreover, combining this with we see that varepsilon: \|\|D_bullet,bullet\|\| to \|N_bullet C\| is n-connected. We have hence shown that the map varepsilon circ alpha: \|(Delta D)_bullet\| to \|N_bullet C\| induces a surjection on pi_k for k le n. But this map is homotopic to iota circ gamma circ alpha, which factors through \|N_bullet C^delta\| cong \|S^delta\|, which we assumed to be n-connected. It follows that pi_k \|N_bullet C\| is 0 for k le n, i.e.~\|N_bullet C\| is n-connected.

Write $C := C(X, \perp)$ and $S := S(X, \perp)$,
    and let $C^\delta$ be $C$ equipped with the discrete topology.
    First, note that $C$ is the poset of simplices of $S$ and hence $B(C^\delta) = |N_\bullet C^\delta|$ is the barycentric subdivision of $|S|$.
    In particular they are homeomorphic, and similarly $|N_\bullet(C^{\perp \ul{y}})^\delta| \cong |S^{\perp \ul{y}}|$.
    From now on all geometric realisations are ``fat'', \emph{i.e.}~we do not quotient by the relations imposed by the degeneracy maps.
    For simplicial sets the fat and thin geometric realisations are always equivalent \cite[Lemma 1.7]{EbertRandalWilliams}.
    
    We define the following bisimplicial subspace of $(N_\bullet C)^\delta \times N_\bullet C$:
    \[
        D_{p,q} := \{ ((\ul{x}^0 \subseteq \dots \subseteq \ul{x}^p),(\ul{y}^0 \subseteq \dots \subseteq \ul{y}^q)) \in N_p C^\delta \times N_q C \;|\; \ul{x}^p \perp \ul{y}^q \}.
    \]
    Note that by $\ul{x}^p \perp \ul{y}^q$ we mean that $\ul{x}^i \perp \ul{y}^j$ for all $i$ and $j$.
    
    We will also need the diagonal of $D_{\bullet, \bullet}$, which is the simplicial space given by 
    $(\Delta D)_p := D_{p,p}$.
    Consider the diagram
    \[
        \begin{tikzcd}[row sep = small]
            && {\|N_\bullet C^\delta\|} \ar[dd, "\iota"] \\
            {\|(\Delta D)_\bullet\|} \ar[r, "\alpha"', "\simeq"] \ar[rru, bend left] \ar[rrd, bend right] & {\|\| D_{\bullet, \bullet} \|\|} \ar[dr, "\varepsilon"'] \ar[ur, "\gamma"] & \\
            && {\|N_\bullet C\|} 
        \end{tikzcd}
    \]
    where the map $\iota$ is the canonical map from the discretisation,
    $\gamma$ projects to the $\ul{x}^i$ and $\varepsilon$ projects to the $\ul{y}^j$.
    The map $\alpha$ is the inclusion of the diagonal and it is a weak equivalence by \cite[Theorem 7.1]{EbertRandalWilliams}.
    
    \noindent
    \textit{Claim:}
    The outside diagram commutes up to homotopy, \emph{i.e.}~$\iota \circ \gamma \circ \alpha \simeq \varepsilon \circ \alpha$.
    
    \textit{Proof of claim:}
    Consider the topological subposet $Q \subset C^\delta \times C$ containing those tuples $(\ul{x}, \ul{y})$ satsifying $\ul{x} \perp \ul{y}$.
    The nerve of $Q$ is isomorphic to the diagonal $\Delta D$:
    the homeomorphism $N_p Q \cong (\Delta D)_p = D_{p,p}$ is given by the tautological map
    \[
        ((\ul{x}^0, \ul{y}^0) \subseteq \dots \subseteq (\ul{x}^p,\ul{y}^p))
        \longmapsto
        ((\ul{x}^0 \subseteq \dots \subseteq \ul{x}^p), (\ul{y}^0 \subseteq \dots \subseteq \ul{y}^p)).
    \]
    The two maps $\iota \circ \gamma \circ \alpha$ and $\varepsilon \circ \alpha$ are obtained as the realisation of the two poset-maps 
    $\mathrm{pr}_1, \mathrm{pr}_2: Q \to C$ defined by $\mathrm{pr}_1(\ul{x}, \ul{y}) := \ul{x}$ and $\mathrm{pr}_2 (\ul{x}, \ul{y}) := \ul{y}$, respectively.

\label{cor:QuillenA}
    Let $(D, \le)$ be a topological poset and 
    $C \subset D$ a sub-poset such that:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For all $d \in D$ the sub-poset 
        $C_{d \le} := \{c \in C \;|\; d \le c\}$
        has a contractible classifying space.
        \item $D$ is left-fibrant, {i.e.}~the map
        \[
            \{(d_0, d_1) \in D^2 \;|\; d_0 \le d_1\} 
            \longrightarrow D, 
            \qquad
            (d_0, d_1) \longmapsto d_0
        \]
        is a Serre fibration.
        \item $C \subset D$ is a union of path components.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then the inclusion $BC \to BD$ is a weak equivalence.

Then f(v) is a reducing sphere in~M which is transverse to all other spheres in~f(K^(0)). We now perform a sequence of surgeries on the spheres in f(K^(0)) to homotope the image of~f into the star of~f(v). For every other vertex w in K the intersection f(v) cap f(w) is a union of circles. The argument from the proof of Proposition 2.7 in \cite{Nariman} works  with some minor changes, since we consider reducing spheres but Nariman considers the larger class of essential spheres that are not boundary parallel. We sketch the proof with modifications here.

    Suppose~$\mathcal{S}(M)$ is nonempty and let~$\kappa \colon M\rightarrow \scl{M}$ be the natural inclusion which caps all 2-sphere boundary components of $M$. 
    We will show that any continuous map~$f\colon S^k\rightarrow \mathcal{S}(M)$ is nulhomotopic.  We may assume that~$f$ is simplicial with respect to some triangulation~$K$ of~$S^k$. As transverse embeddings are residual \cite[Theorem 2.1]{Hirsch}, after a simplicial homotopy we may assume that the images of the vertices of~$K$ under~$f$ are pairwise transverse. 
    Choose a vertex~$v\in K$.
    Then $f(v)$ is a reducing sphere in~$M$ which is transverse to all other spheres in~$f(K^{(0)})$.
    
    We now perform a sequence of surgeries on the spheres in $f(K^{(0)})$ to homotope the image of~$f$ into the star of~$f(v)$. 
    For every other vertex $w \in K$ the intersection $f(v) \cap f(w)$ is a union of circles.
    Let~$N$ be total number of intersection circles in $f(v)$, i.e.~the number of circles in $f(v)\cap f(w)$, summed over all $w \neq v$.
    Consider all such circles, take a maximal disjoint family, and consider an innermost circle $C$ in this family. (Here, innermost means that~$C$ bounds a disk in~$f(v)$ containing no other circle in the maximal collection.) 
    Then $C$ is an intersection between $f(v)$ and a reducing sphere~$f(w)$ for $w \in K$.
    For the surgery step, we need to show that if we surger~$f(w)$ at $C$ with respect to the transverse sphere~$f(v)$ to obtain two spheres~$S_0$ and~$S_1$ (see \cite[Figure 2]{Nariman}) then at least one of~$S_0$ or~$S_1$ is still reducing.
    Since~$f(w)$ and~$f(v)$ lie in the interior of~$M$, we may perform the surgery entirely in~$\interior{M}$. Passing to~$\scl{M}$ via~$\kappa$, we may perform the same surgery away from the added 3-balls. By assumption,~$f(w)$ and~$f(v)$ are reducing, hence essential in~$\scl{M}$ by Remark \ref{rem - essential does not bound}. 
    In $\pi_2(\scl{M},p)$ we have $[S_0]+[S_1]=[f(w)]$. As $[f(w)]$ is nontrivial, at least one of $[S_0]$ or $[S_1]$ is nontrivial. 
    Thus we can pick $i \in \{0,1\}$ such that the sphere $S_i$ is still essential in~$\scl{M}$ and therefore reducing in $M$.
    
    The map $f$ is now replaced with a homotopic map $f'$
    that agrees with $f$ on all vertices except $w$, but sends $w$ to $S_i$ instead of $f(w)$.
    (The original map $f$ sends all vertices in $\mathrm{link}_K(w)$ to spheres disjoint from $S_i$ since $C$ was chosen to be innermost,
    and after a small translation $S_i$ is also disjoint from $f(w)$, so $f'$ sends all of $\mathrm{star}_K(w)$ to the star of $f(w)$ in $\mathcal{S}(M)$.
    This is what allows us to find this homotopy --
    see \cite[Figure 4]{BoydBregman22} for a schematic.)
    Since $f'(w) = S_i$ no longer intersects $f(v)$ at $C$, for this new map $f'$ the number of intersections $N$ has been reduced by one, so by induction we can reduce $N$ to zero i.e.~until $f$ sends all of $K$ into the star of $f(v)$. 
    Hence, $f$ is nullhomotopic and~$\mathcal{S}(M)$ is contractible as required.

By assumption,~f(w) and~f(v) are reducing, hence essential in~sclM by Remark . In pi_2(sclM,p) we have [S_0]+[S_1]=[f(w)]. As [f(w)] is nontrivial, at least one of [S_0] or [S_1] is nontrivial. Thus we can pick i in \0,1\ such that the sphere S_i is still essential in~sclM and therefore reducing in M. The map f is now replaced with a homotopic map f' that agrees with f on all vertices except w, but sends w to S_i instead of f(w). (The original map f sends all vertices in link_K(w) to spheres disjoint from S_i since C was chosen to be innermost, and after a small translation S_i is also disjoint from f(w), so f' sends all of star_K(w) to the star of f(w) in S(M). This is what allows us to find this homotopy -- see for a schematic.) Since f'(w) = S_i no longer intersects f(v) at C, for this new map f' the number of intersections N has been reduced by one, so by induction we can reduce N to zero i.e.~until f sends all of K into the star of f(v). Hence, f is nullhomotopic and~S(M) is contractible as required.

nodes.statement: Cut^neq emptyset_bullet(M) is non-empty, since we assumed that~sclM was not irreducible. Following the framework of Section , let~X be the subspace of Sub(S^2, M) consisting of reducing spheres, and~perp be the symmetric and anti-reflexive relation on~X given by~S_0perp S_1 iff~S_0cap S_1=emptyset. Then Cut^neq emptyset_bullet(M) is the nerve of the associated topological poset C(X,perp) from Definition~. We now apply the adaptation of the discretisation technique of Galatius and Randal-Williams given in~Proposition . First note that S(X,perp) (Definition ) is contractible since it is precisely the complex S(M), which is contractible by Theorem~. Hence condition~(1) of Proposition~ is satisfied for all~n. For condition~(2) we fix a cut system Sigma in Cut^neq emptyset_bullet(M) (which will function as~uly in the proposition) and consider the simplicial complex~S(X,perp)^perp Sigma. This complex is contractible -- for any map~f:S^k to S(X,perp)^perp Sigma, there exists a sphere~S disjoint from all vertices in im (f) (for example, take S to be a parallel copy of a sphere in~Sigma). S is therefore a vertex in S(X,perp)^perp Sigma which acts as a cone point for~im (f) and thus S(X,perp)^perp Sigmasimeq *. Therefore (2) is also satisfied for all n. Applying Proposition~ gives that~\|Cut^neq emptyset_bullet(M)\| is n-connected for all n, and thus contractible.

$\mathrm{Cut}^{\neq \emptyset}_\bullet(M)$ is non-empty, since we assumed that~$\scl{M}$ was not irreducible.
    Following the framework of Section \ref{section - discretization}, let~$X$ be the subspace of $\mathrm{Sub}(S^2, M)$ consisting of reducing spheres, and~$\perp$ be the symmetric and anti-reflexive relation on~$X$ given by~$S_0\perp S_1$ iff~$S_0\cap S_1=\emptyset$. 
    Then $\mathrm{Cut}^{\neq \emptyset}_\bullet(M)$ is the nerve of the associated topological poset $C(X,\perp)$ from Definition~\ref{defn - C/S(X, perp)}. 
    We now apply the adaptation of the discretisation technique of Galatius and Randal-Williams \cite{GalatiusRandalWilliams} given in~Proposition \ref{prop - poset discretization}. First note that $S(X,\perp)$ (Definition \ref{defn - C/S(X, perp)}) is contractible since it is precisely the complex $\mathcal{S}(M)$, which is contractible by Theorem~\ref{thm: S(M)-contractible}. Hence condition~$(1)$ of Proposition~\ref{prop - poset discretization} is satisfied for all~$n$. 
    For condition~$(2)$ we fix a cut system $\Sigma \in \mathrm{Cut}^{\neq \emptyset}_\bullet(M)$ (which will function as~$\ul{y}$ in the proposition) and consider the simplicial complex~$S(X,\perp)^{\perp \Sigma}$. This complex is contractible -- for any map~$f:S^k \to S(X,\perp)^{\perp \Sigma}$, there exists a sphere~$S$ disjoint from all vertices in $\mathrm{im} (f)$ (for example, take $S$ to be a parallel copy of a sphere in~$\Sigma$). $S$ is therefore a vertex in $S(X,\perp)^{\perp \Sigma}$ which acts as a cone point for~$\mathrm{im} (f)$ and thus $S(X,\perp)^{\perp \Sigma}\simeq *$. 
    Therefore $(2)$ is also satisfied for all $n$. Applying Proposition~\ref{prop - poset discretization} gives that~$\|\mathrm{Cut}^{\neq \emptyset}_\bullet(M)\|$ is $n$-connected for all $n$, and thus contractible.

nodes.statement: Let q be the number of prime factors in M. For p ge q the poset qsepp(M) contains the empty cut system, which is initial and hence acts as a cone point for \|qsepp_bullet(M)\|. We show that \|qsepp_bullet(M)\| to \|qsepp+1_bullet(M)\| is a homotopy equivalence for all pge 1. We invoke Quillen's Theorem A for topological categories as recalled in Corollary , noting that (3) is true since connected components correspond to isotopy classes of cut systems, and (2) is true because the map \[ Cut_1(M) = \Sigma_0 subseteq Sigma_1 in Cut(M)\ to Cut(M), (Sigma_0 subseteq Sigma_1) mapsto Sigma_0 \] is a Diff(M)-equivariant map into a Diff(M)-locally retractile space and hence a fiber bundle by creflem:locally-retractile(1). It therefore suffices to show (1): the slice category of the inclusion functor at every object Upsilon in qsepp+1(M) has a contractible classifying space. In the case at hand this slice category is the poset \[ qsepp(M)_Upsilon subseteq = \ Sigma in qsepp(M) \;|\; Upsilon subseteq Sigma\. \] Any separating system Sigma containing Upsilon decomposes as the disjoint union Sigma = Upsilon sqcup Upsilon^c and it will suffice to keep track of Upsilon^c. Note that while Upsilon^c is p-separating in Msmashmid Upsilon, it may contain spheres which are not reducing in M smashmid Upsilon (for example, they may be boundary parallel, if they were parallel to a sphere in~Upsilon). We introduce the following modification of~qsepp(M) to account for this. Let N be a 3-manifold and let Bsubset partial N be a union of 2-sphere boundary components. Let N_sclB denote be the manifold obtained by filling each 2-sphere of B with a disk. Define C^pfleq p(N,B) to be collections of disjointly embedded spheres in N that are essential in~N_sclB and~p-separating, and let C_bullet^pfleq p(N,B) be the nerve of the associated poset. In particular, qsepp(N) = C^pf le p(N, partial N) subseteq C^pfleq p(N,B) but the essential spheres appearing in collections in C^pfleq p(N, B) are not necessarily reducing. Let U be a connected component of Msmashmid Upsilon. Each boundary sphere of M lies in a unique such component U. Let B_U be the union of all 2-spheres in partial U that come from partial M. Then there is a homeomorphism \[ qsepp(M)_Upsilon subseteq cong prod_U in pi_0(Msmashmid Upsilon) C^pfleq p(U,B_U). \] Since~Upsilon in qsepp+1(M), the components of sclM smashmid Upsilon have at most~p+1 prime factors. Therefore, for each U there are two possibilities: item if sclU has at most p prime factors, then C^pfleq p(U,B_U) contains the empty sphere system, which is an initial object and hence \|C_bullet^pfleq p(U, B_U)\| is contractible. item If sclU has exactly p+1 prime factors, then every~Sigma in C^pfleq p(U,B_U) must contain at least one reducing sphere. Therefore the inclusion Cut^neq emptyset(U)subseteq C^pfleq p(U,B_U) admits a retraction F: C^pfleq p(U,B_U)to Cut^neq emptyset(U) that forgets spheres which are not reducing. By Lemma~ this is homotopic to the identity map, so Cut^neq emptyset_bullet(U) is a deformation retract of C^pfleq p(U,B_U). Since \|Cut^neq emptyset_bullet(U)\| is contractible by Proposition~, it follows that \|C_bullet^pfleq p(U,B_U)\| is contractible. Therefore, \|C_bullet^pfleq p(U,B_U)\| is always contractible. The fat geometric realisation of a product of simplicial spaces is equivalent to the product of the fat geometric realisations , so \|qsepp_bullet(M)_Upsilonsubseteq\| is contractible, and applying crefcor:QuillenA completes the proof.
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $q$ be the number of prime factors in $M$. 
    For $p \ge q$ the poset $\qsep{p}(M)$ contains the empty cut system, which is initial and hence acts as a cone point for $\|\qsep{p}_\bullet(M)\|$.
    We show that $\|\qsep{p}_\bullet(M)\| \to \|\qsep{p+1}_\bullet(M)\|$ is a homotopy equivalence for all $p\ge 1$.
    
    We invoke Quillen's Theorem A for topological categories \cite[Theorem 4.8]{EbertRandalWilliams} as recalled in Corollary \ref{cor:QuillenA},  noting that \ref{cor:QuillenA}(3) is true since connected components correspond to isotopy classes of cut systems, and \ref{cor:QuillenA}(2) is true
    because the map
    \[
        \mathrm{Cut}_1(M) = \{\Sigma_0 \subseteq \Sigma_1 \in \mathrm{Cut}(M)\} \to \mathrm{Cut}(M),
        \qquad
        (\Sigma_0 \subseteq \Sigma_1) \mapsto \Sigma_0
    \]
    is a $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$-equivariant map into a $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$-locally retractile space and hence a fiber bundle by \cref{lem:locally-retractile}(1).
    
    It therefore suffices to show \ref{cor:QuillenA}(1): the slice category of the inclusion functor at every object $\Upsilon \in \qsep{p+1}(M)$ has a contractible classifying space.
    In the case at hand this slice category is the poset
    \[
        \qsep{p}(M)_{\Upsilon \subseteq} = \{ \Sigma \in \qsep{p}(M) \;|\; \Upsilon \subseteq \Sigma\}.
    \]
    Any separating system $\Sigma$ containing $\Upsilon$ decomposes as the disjoint union $\Sigma = \Upsilon \sqcup \Upsilon^c$ and it will suffice to keep track of $\Upsilon^c$.
    Note that while $\Upsilon^c$ is $p$-separating in $M\smash{\mid} \Upsilon$, it may contain spheres which are not reducing in $M \smash{\mid} \Upsilon$ (for example, they may be boundary parallel, if they were parallel to a sphere in~$\Upsilon$).  
    
    We introduce the following modification of~$\qsep{p}(M)$ to account for this.  Let $N$ be a 3-manifold and let $B\subset \partial N$ be a union of 2-sphere boundary components.  Let $N_{\scl{B}}$ denote be the manifold obtained by filling each 2-sphere of $B$ with a disk. Define $C^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}(N,B)$ to be collections of disjointly embedded spheres in $N$ that are essential in~$N_{\scl{B}}$ and~$p$-separating, and let $C_\bullet^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}(N,B)$ be the nerve of the associated poset. 
    In particular, $\qsep{p}(N) = C^{\mathrm{pf} \le p}(N, \partial N) \subseteq C^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}(N,B)$ but the essential spheres appearing in collections in $C^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}(N, B)$ are not necessarily reducing.
    
    
    Let $U$ be a connected component of $M\smash{\mid} \Upsilon$. Each boundary sphere of $M$ lies in a unique such component $U$. Let $B_U$ be the union of all 2-spheres in $\partial U$ that come from $\partial M$. Then there is a homeomorphism
    \[
        \qsep{p}(M)_{\Upsilon \subseteq}
        \cong \prod_{U \in \pi_0(M\smash{\mid} \Upsilon)} C^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}(U,B_U).
    \]
    
    Since~$\Upsilon \in \qsep{p+1}(M)$, the components of $\scl{M \smash{\mid} \Upsilon}$ have at most~$p+1$ prime factors. Therefore, for each $U$ there are two possibilities:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item if $\scl{U}$ has at most $p$ prime factors, then $C^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}({U},B_U)$ contains the empty sphere system, which is an initial object and hence $\|C_\bullet^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}({U}, B_U)\|$ is contractible.
        \item If $\scl{U}$ has exactly $p+1$ prime factors, then every~$\Sigma \in C^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}({U},B_U)$ must contain at least one reducing sphere. 
        Therefore the inclusion $\mathrm{Cut}^{\neq \emptyset}({U})\subseteq C^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}({U},B_U)$ admits a retraction $F: C^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}(U,B_U)\to \mathrm{Cut}^{\neq \emptyset}({U})$ that forgets spheres which are not reducing. 
        By Lemma~\ref{lem:poset-natural-transformation=homotopy} this is homotopic to the identity map, so $\mathrm{Cut}^{\neq \emptyset}_\bullet({U})$ is a deformation retract of $C^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}({U},B_U)$. Since $\|\mathrm{Cut}^{\neq \emptyset}_\bullet({U})\|$ is contractible by Proposition~\ref{prop:ess-red-contratible}, it follows that $\|C_\bullet^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}({U},B_U)\|$ is contractible.
    \end{itemize}
    Therefore, $\|C_\bullet^{\mathrm{pf}\leq p}({U},B_U)\|$ is always contractible.
    The fat geometric realisation of a product of simplicial spaces is equivalent to the product of the fat geometric realisations \cite[Theorem 7.1]{EbertRandalWilliams}, so $\|\qsep{p}_{\bullet}(M)_{\Upsilon\subseteq}\|$ is contractible, and applying \cref{cor:QuillenA} completes the proof.

In the case at hand this slice category is the poset \[ qsepp(M)_Upsilon subseteq = \ Sigma in qsepp(M) \;|\; Upsilon subseteq Sigma\. \] Any separating system Sigma containing Upsilon decomposes as the disjoint union Sigma = Upsilon sqcup Upsilon^c and it will suffice to keep track of Upsilon^c. Note that while Upsilon^c is p-separating in Msmashmid Upsilon, it may contain spheres which are not reducing in M smashmid Upsilon (for example, they may be boundary parallel, if they were parallel to a sphere in~Upsilon). We introduce the following modification of~qsepp(M) to account for this. Let N be a 3-manifold and let Bsubset partial N be a union of 2-sphere boundary components. Let N_sclB denote be the manifold obtained by filling each 2-sphere of B with a disk. Define C^pfleq p(N,B) to be collections of disjointly embedded spheres in N that are essential in~N_sclB and~p-separating, and let C_bullet^pfleq p(N,B) be the nerve of the associated poset. In particular, qsepp(N) = C^pf le p(N, partial N) subseteq C^pfleq p(N,B) but the essential spheres appearing in collections in C^pfleq p(N, B) are not necessarily reducing. Let U be a connected component of Msmashmid Upsilon. Each boundary sphere of M lies in a unique such component U. Let B_U be the union of all 2-spheres in partial U that come from partial M. Then there is a homeomorphism \[ qsepp(M)_Upsilon subseteq cong prod_U in pi_0(Msmashmid Upsilon) C^pfleq p(U,B_U). \] Since~Upsilon in qsepp+1(M), the components of sclM smashmid Upsilon have at most~p+1 prime factors. Therefore, for each U there are two possibilities: item if sclU has at most p prime factors, then C^pfleq p(U,B_U) contains the empty sphere system, which is an initial object and hence \|C_bullet^pfleq p(U, B_U)\| is contractible. item If sclU has exactly p+1 prime factors, then every~Sigma in C^pfleq p(U,B_U) must contain at least one reducing sphere. Therefore the inclusion Cut^neq emptyset(U)subseteq C^pfleq p(U,B_U) admits a retraction F: C^pfleq p(U,B_U)to Cut^neq emptyset(U) that forgets spheres which are not reducing. By Lemma~ this is homotopic to the identity map, so Cut^neq emptyset_bullet(U) is a deformation retract of C^pfleq p(U,B_U). Since \|Cut^neq emptyset_bullet(U)\| is contractible by Proposition~, it follows that \|C_bullet^pfleq p(U,B_U)\| is contractible. Therefore, \|C_bullet^pfleq p(U,B_U)\| is always contractible. The fat geometric realisation of a product of simplicial spaces is equivalent to the product of the fat geometric realisations , so \|qsepp_bullet(M)_Upsilonsubseteq\| is contractible, and applying crefcor:QuillenA completes the proof.

\label{defn:parallel}

nodes.statement: Suppose such an orientation-reversing isotopy exists. By isotopy extension, we can find an isotopy from Id_M to a diffeomorphism h reversing the coorientation on S. Since M is orientable, h must reverse the orientation on S as well. We first claim S separates M. If not, there is a simple closed curve gammasubset M that intersects S in exactly one point. Hence gamma and S are duals for the intersection pairing on M, so [S]in H_2(M) generates a nontrivial free factor. But then h_*[S]=-[S], contradicting hsimeqId_M. So we may assume S separates M. Since h reverses the coorientation on S, it exchanges the two (necessarily homeomorphic) components M_0 and M_1 of Msmashmid S. If neither M_0 nor M_1 are simply connected, then pi_1(M_0)cong pi_1(M_1)cong G for some nontrivial G. Moreover, pi_1(M)cong G*G and h_* exchanges the two factors. Since h_* preserves the kernel of the natural homomorphism G*Grightarrow Gtimes G, it induces an automorphism of Gtimes G, which cannot be not inner, since no nontrivial element of Gtimes\1\ is conjugate to an element of \1\times G. Thus, h_*colon pi_1(M) to pi_1(M) is not inner, again contradicting hsimeq Id_M. Finally, if M_0 and M_1 are simply connected, they are each homeomorphic to S^3setminus (coprod_kinteriorD^3), and since S is essential, we must have kgeq 2. But then h would have to permute the boundary spheres, and it cannot because it is isotopic to the identity.

Hence $\gamma$ and $S$ are duals for the intersection pairing on $M$, so $[S]\in H_2(M)$ generates a nontrivial free factor. But then $h_*[S]=-[S]$, contradicting $h\simeq\textrm{Id}_M$.

    But then $h$ would have to permute the boundary spheres, and it cannot because it is isotopic to the identity.

nodes.statement: The Diff_partial(M)-equivariant map \[ pcolon Emb_S_0times\0\( S_0 times [0,1], M) to Sub(S_0, interiorM), i mapsto i(S_0 times \1\) \] is a fiber bundle because Sub(S_0, M) is Diff_partial(M)-locally retractile by crefcor:umb-retractile. Moreover, by the definition of parallel, the image of this map is exactly the connected component P(S_0; M) subset Sub(S_0, interiorM). Let S_1 in P(S_0; M) be some unparametrised sphere parallel to S_0. The fiber p at some unparametrised sphere S_1 in P(S_0; M), which is parallel to S_0, is the space of those embeddings iotacolon S_0 times [0,1] hookrightarrow M that are the identity on S_0 times \0\ and send S_0 times \1\ to S_1. The image of such an embedding is always exactly the connected component U subset M smashmid S_1 that lies between S_0 and S_1. U is necessarily diffeomorphic to S^2 times [0,1]. Specifying another embedding iota' in p^-1(S_1) is hence equivalent to specifying a diffeomorphism S_0 times [0,1] cong U that is the identity on S_0 times \0\. Therefore we have a fiber sequence \[ Diff_S_0times\0\(S_0 times [0,1]) to Emb_S_0 times \0\(S_0 times [0, 1], M) to P(S_0; M). \] The left term is the group of pseudo-isotopies of S^2, which is contractible by Hatcher's proof of the Smale conjecture . The middle term is the space of collars of S_0 in M, which is also contractible by , as recalled in crefthm:contractible-collars. Therefore P(S_0; M) is contractible.

The $\mathrm{Diff}_\partial(M)$-equivariant map
    \[
        p\colon \mathrm{Emb}_{S_0\times\{0\}}( S_0 \times [0,1], M)  \to
        \mathrm{Sub}(S_0, \interior{M}), \qquad
        i \mapsto i(S_0 \times \{1\})
    \]
    is a fiber bundle because $\mathrm{Sub}(S_0, M)$ is $\mathrm{Diff}_\partial(M)$-locally retractile by \cref{cor:umb-retractile}.
    Moreover, by the definition of parallel, the image of this map is exactly the connected component $P(S_0; M) \subset \mathrm{Sub}(S_0, \interior{M})$.
    Let $S_1 \in P(S_0; M)$ be some unparametrised sphere parallel to $S_0$.
    The fiber $p$ at some unparametrised sphere $S_1 \in P(S_0; M)$, which is parallel to $S_0$,
    is the space of those embeddings
    $\iota\colon S_0 \times [0,1] \hookrightarrow M$
    that are the identity on $S_0 \times \{0\}$ and send $S_0 \times \{1\}$ to $S_1$.
    The image of such an embedding is always exactly the connected component $U \subset M \smash{\mid} S_1$ that lies between $S_0$ and $S_1$. $U$ is necessarily diffeomorphic to $S^2 \times [0,1]$.
    Specifying another embedding $\iota' \in p^{-1}(S_1)$ is hence equivalent to specifying a diffeomorphism $S_0 \times [0,1] \cong U$ that is the identity on $S_0 \times \{0\}$.
    Therefore we have a fiber sequence
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}_{S_0\times\{0\}}(S_0 \times [0,1]) \to \mathrm{Emb}_{S_0 \times \{0\}}(S_0 \times [0, 1], M) \to P(S_0; M).
    \]
    The left term is the group of pseudo-isotopies of $S^2$, which is contractible by Hatcher's proof of the Smale conjecture \cite{Hatcher}.
    The middle term is the space of collars of $S_0$ in $M$, which is also contractible by \cite{Cerf}, as recalled in \cref{thm:contractible-collars}.
    Therefore $P(S_0; M)$ is contractible.

Then the topological poset Sep^L(M) is defined as follows. \label{defn:L}
    For a sphere system $\Sigma$ we let $L(\Sigma) \subseteq \Sigma$ denote the sphere system that selects the left-most sphere from each isotopy class represented in $\Sigma$.

nodes.statement: By crefcor:umb-retractile, Sep(M) is a locally Diff(M)-retractile space and so by creflem:locally-retractile(1) any Diff(M)-equivariant map into it is a locally trivial fibration. For an isotopy class a in pi_0Sub(S^2, M), let Sep^a(M) subset Sep(M) denote the subspace of those separating systems Sigma such that the number of spheres of Sigma that are in the isotopy class a is at least 2. This only depends on the isotopy class of Sigma, hence Sep^a(M) is a union of path components of Sep(M). Then we can define a map \[ R_acolon Sep^a(M) to Sep(M) \] that forgets the left-most sphere from the isotopy class a. This map is again a fiber bundle because Sep(M) is locally Diff(M)-retractile. Each path component of Sep^L(M) belongs to Sep^a(M) for only finitely many a, hence restricted to each path component the map R is equal to a finite composite of maps of the form R_a. Thus, it will suffice to show that each R_a is a trivial Serre fibration. We therefore have to show that the fiber R_a^-1(Sigma) is contractible at any Sigma in Sep(M) in the image of R_a. A point in this fiber is of the form Sigma sqcup S for some S in Sub(S^2, M) such that S is disjoint from Sigma, S is in the isotopy class a, and (within Sigma sqcup S) S is the left-most sphere in its isotopy class. Let S_0 be the left-most sphere in Sigma that is in the isotopy class a. Then we can equivalently write the fiber as the subspace of those unparametrised spheres that are parallel to S_0 subset partial (Msmashmid Sigma). (Here there are two ways of thinking of S_0 as a sphere in the boundary of Msmashmid Sigma. We choose the one that corresponds to the left side of S_0 subset M.) \[ R_a^-1(Sigma) cong \S in Sub(S^2, (M smashmid Sigma)^circ) \;|\; S parallel to S_0\ \] Contractibility now follows from creflem:boundary-parallel-spheres. To prove the final claim, we first consider the commutative square \[ Sep^L_n(M) ar[r, "R_n"] ar[d] & Sep_n(M) ar[d] \\ Sep^L_0(M) ar[r, "R_0"] & Sep_0(M) \] where the vertical maps send (Sigma_0 subseteq dots subseteq Sigma_n) to Sigma_n. These vertical maps are finite coverings by creflem:face-map-is-finite-covering and the horizontal map induces a bijection on fibers, so the square is a pullback and hence R_n is also a trivial Serre fibration. Fat geometric realisation preserves weak equivalences so \|R\| is a weak equivalence. The proof for L is entirely analogous.
nodes.raw_latex:
By \cref{cor:umb-retractile}, $\mathrm{Sep}(M)$ is a locally $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$-retractile space and so by \cref{lem:locally-retractile}(1) any $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$-equivariant map into it is a locally trivial fibration.

    For an isotopy class $a \in \pi_0\mathrm{Sub}(S^2, M)$, let $\mathrm{Sep}^a(M) \subset \mathrm{Sep}(M)$ denote the subspace of those separating systems $\Sigma$ such that the number of spheres of $\Sigma$ that are in the isotopy class $a$ is at least $2$. This only depends on the isotopy class of $\Sigma$, hence $\mathrm{Sep}^a(M)$ is a union of path components of $\mathrm{Sep}(M)$.
    Then we can define a map
    \[
        R_a\colon \mathrm{Sep}^a(M) \to \mathrm{Sep}(M) 
    \]
    that forgets the left-most sphere from the isotopy class $a$. 
    This map is again a fiber bundle because $\mathrm{Sep}(M)$ is locally $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$-retractile. Each path component of $\mathrm{Sep}^{\mathrm{L}}(M)$ belongs to $\mathrm{Sep}^a(M)$ for only finitely many $a$, hence restricted to each path component the map $R$ is equal to a finite composite of maps of the form $R_a$. Thus, it will suffice to show that each $R_a$ is a trivial Serre fibration.



    We therefore have to show that the fiber $R_a^{-1}(\Sigma)$ is contractible at any $\Sigma \in \mathrm{Sep}(M)$ in the image of $R_a$.
    A point in this fiber is of the form $\Sigma \sqcup S$ for some $S \in \mathrm{Sub}(S^2, M)$ such that $S$ is disjoint from $\Sigma$, $S$ is in the isotopy class $a$, and (within $\Sigma \sqcup S$) $S$ is the left-most sphere in its isotopy class.
    Let $S_0$ be the left-most sphere in $\Sigma$ that is in the isotopy class $a$.
    Then we can equivalently write the fiber as the subspace  of those unparametrised spheres that are parallel to $S_0 \subset \partial (M\smash{\mid} \Sigma)$.
    (Here there are two ways of thinking of $S_0$ as a sphere in the boundary of $M\smash{\mid} \Sigma$. We choose the one that corresponds to the left side of $S_0 \subset M$.)
    \[
        R_a^{-1}(\Sigma) \cong 
        \{S \in \mathrm{Sub}(S^2, (M \smash{\mid} \Sigma)^\circ) \;|\; S \text{ parallel to } S_0\}
    \]
    Contractibility now follows from \cref{lem:boundary-parallel-spheres}.

    To prove the final claim, we first consider the commutative square
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
        \mathrm{Sep}^{\mathrm{L}}_n(M) \ar[r, "R_n"] \ar[d] & \mathrm{Sep}_n(M) \ar[d] \\
        \mathrm{Sep}^{\mathrm{L}}_0(M) \ar[r, "R_0"] & \mathrm{Sep}_0(M)
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    where the vertical maps send $(\Sigma_0 \subseteq \dots \subseteq \Sigma_n)$ to $\Sigma_n$.
    These vertical maps are finite coverings by \cref{lem:face-map-is-finite-covering} and the horizontal map induces a bijection on fibers, so the square is a pullback and hence $R_n$ is also a trivial Serre fibration. 
    Fat geometric realisation preserves weak equivalences \cite[Theorem 2.2]{EbertRandalWilliams} so $\|R\|$ is a weak equivalence.
    The proof for $L$ is entirely analogous.

The top triangle in this diagram commutes. Consider the three maps \[ L, F, R colon Sep^L(M) longrightarrow Sep(M) \] where F is the forgetful map (i.e.~the inclusion on underlying spaces). For every Sigma we have inclusions L(Sigma) subset F(Sigma) = Sigma supset R(Sigma). Therefore Lemma provides us with homotopies |L| simeq |F| simeq |R|, so the following diagram commutes up to homotopy. \[ [column sep = large] \|Sep^L,2_bullet(M)\| ar[r, "\|I\|"] ar[d, "\|L\|"'] & \|Sep^L_bullet(M)\| ar[dl, "\|L\|"'] ar[d, "\|R\|"] \\ \|Sep^nparallel_bullet(M)\| ar[r, "\|I\|"] & \|Sep_bullet(M)\| \] By creflem:forget-left-most-sphere the two vertical maps in the above square are weak equivalences. nodes.raw_latex:

nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem combines the results of several authors spanning decades. For Haken geometric 3-manifolds, it follows from results of Hatcher and, independently, Ivanov on spaces of incompressible surfaces. Hatcher and Ivanov's work covers all Haken cases and thus all cases when M has non-empty boundary, all cases with Sol-geometry, and many of the hyperbolic and Seifert-fibered cases except possibly when the base-orbifold is homeomorphic to S^2. For M=S^3, Theorem follows from Hatcher . It was proven for quotients of S^3 containing one-sided incompressible Klein bottles (prismatic and quaternionic) and lens spaces other than RP^3 using topological techniques . Bamler--Kleiner used Ricci flow techniques to prove the remaining cases (tetrahedral, octahedral, icosahedral, and RP^3) and gave a unified proof for all spherical 3-manifolds. In particular, their approach offers a new proof of the Smale conjecture.

For Haken geometric 3-manifolds, it follows from results of Hatcher \cite{Hatcher76} and, independently, Ivanov \cite{Ivanov76} on spaces of incompressible surfaces. By Theorem 3.15 of \cite{HKMR12} all orientable Haken Seifert-fibered manifolds that are not exceptional are fiber-rigid.
    In fact, their theorem says that for non-exceptional cases $\mathrm{SF}(M;[\varphi])$ is contractible for any choice of $\varphi$.
    Thus it remains to prove that for $K\widetilde{\times}I$ and $D(K\widetilde{\times}I)$ there exists a fibering $\varphi$ for which $\mathrm{Diff}^f(M; [\varphi]) \to \mathrm{Diff}(M)$ is surjective on $\pi_0$.
    
If $M=K\widetilde{\times}I$, then $M\simeq K$ so $\pi_1(M)\cong \pi :=\langle a,t\mid tat^{-1}=a^{-1}\rangle$. 
By Waldhausen's theorem \cite{Waldhausen68}, $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ is isomorphic to the subgroup of $\mathrm{Out}(\pi)$ preserving $\pi_1(\partial M)$.
In the case at hand $\pi_1(\partial M) \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$ 
is the subgroup $\langle a, t^2\rangle \leq \pi$, which is characteristic, so $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(M)\cong \mathrm{Out}(\pi)\cong \mathbb{Z}/2\times\mathbb{Z}/2$. 
The generators of $\mathrm{Out}(\pi)$ are $\sigma_1\colon t\mapsto t^{-1}$, $a\mapsto a$ and $\sigma_2\colon t\mapsto ta$, $a\mapsto a$.
There are two distinct Seifert fiberings $\varphi_1$, $\varphi_2$ of $M$ corresponding to the two maximal normal infinite cyclic subgroups of $\pi$, namely $\langle a\rangle$ and $\langle t^2\rangle$, respectively. 
The base surface of $\varphi_1$ is M\"obius strip and there are no singular fibers. 
The base orbifold of $\varphi_2$ is a disk with two cone points of order 2. 
These two cone points correspond to the conjugacy classes of $t$ and $ta$ respectively. 
Both $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ can be realised by diffeomorphisms of $K\widetilde{\times}I$ that preserve both fiberings: $\sigma_1$ is a reflection that reverses the orientation of each fiber of $\varphi_2$, preserving each setwise, while $\sigma_2$ rotates each fibers of $\varphi_1$ by $180^\circ$ and permutes the fibers of $\varphi_2$, exchanging the two singular fibers (see Figure \ref{fig:Twisted Klein}). Thus $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}^f(M;[\varphi_i])$ surjects onto $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ for $i=1,2$. Using either $\varphi_1$ or $\varphi_2$ proves the theorem in this case.


Finally, consider $M=D(K\widetilde{\times}I)$, the double of $K\widetilde{\times}I$.  Then $M$ supports a flat metric, and by \cite[Theorem 1]{CharlapVasquez}, the group of affine automorphisms $\mathrm{Aff}(M)$ fits into a short exact sequence\[1\rightarrow \mathrm{Aff}_0(M)\rightarrow \mathrm{Aff}(M)\rightarrow \mathrm{Aff}(M)/\mathrm{Aff}_0(M)\rightarrow 1,\] where $\mathrm{Aff}_0(M)= \mathrm{Isom}_0(M)$, and $\mathrm{Aff}(M)/\mathrm{Aff}_0(M)\cong \mathrm{Out}(\pi_1(M))$.  Therefore by \cref{thm:Gen-Smale} and Waldhausen's theorem \cite{Waldhausen68}, the inclusion $\mathrm{Aff}(M)\rightarrow \mathrm{Diff}(M)$ is a homotopy equivalence.
On the other hand, the quotient map  $\varphi_0\colon M\rightarrow M/\mathrm{Aff}_0(M)$ is a Seifert fibering with base surface a sphere with 4 cone points of order 2. Since $\mathrm{Aff}_0(M)$ is normal in $\mathrm{Aff}(M)$, every element of $\mathrm{Out}(\pi_1(M))\cong \mathrm{Aff}(M)/\mathrm{Aff}_0(M)$ is realised by a fiber-preserving diffeomorphism of $M$. Thus, $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(M;[\varphi_0])\rightarrow \mathrm{Out}(\pi_1(M))\cong \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ is surjective.

The standard action of GL_3(Z) on R^3 preserves the Z^3 lattice, hence descends to a group of diffeomorphisms of T^3=R^3/Z^3. By crefthm:Gen-Smale, the group of translations of T^3, which is equal to Isom_0(T^3) and which we denote by T^3, is homotopy equivalent to Diff_0(T^3). Hence the inclusion T^3rtimesGL_3(Z)hookrightarrow Diff(T^3) is a homotopy equivalence. Let Fr(T^3) be the space of frames on T^3. There is a diffeomorphism Fr(T^3)cong T^3times GL_3(R), and using the standard flat metric on T^3, this diffeomorphism is compatible with the action of T^3rtimes GL_3(Z): the translation action is trivial on the GL_3(R) factor and freely transitive on T^3, while GL_3(Z) acts on GL_3(R) via the standard right action. In particular, the action is free with quotient GL_3(R)/GL_3(Z). Since $T^3$ is closed and Haken, Waldhausen's theorem \cite{Waldhausen68} implies that the natural map $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(T^3)\rightarrow \mathrm{Out}(\pi_1(T^3))\cong \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ is an isomorphism. The standard action of $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ preserves the $\mathbb{Z}^3$ lattice, hence descends to a group of diffeomorphisms of $T^3=\mathbb{R}^3/\mathbb{Z}^3$.
    By  \cref{thm:Gen-Smale}, the group of translations of $T^3$, which is equal to $\mathrm{Isom}_0(T^3)$ and which we denote by $\mathbb{T}^3$, is homotopy equivalent to $\mathrm{Diff}_0(T^3)$. Hence the inclusion $\mathbb{T}^3\rtimes\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})\hookrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}(T^3)$ is a homotopy equivalence.
    
    Let $\mathrm{Fr}(T^3)$ be the space of frames on $T^3$. There is a diffeomorphism $\mathrm{Fr}(T^3)\cong T^3\times \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{R})$, and using the standard flat metric on $T^3$, this diffeomorphism is compatible with the action of $\mathbb{T}^3\rtimes \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$: the translation action is trivial on the $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{R})$ factor and freely transitive on $T^3$, while $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ acts on $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{R})$ via the standard right action. In particular, the action is free with quotient $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$. 
    By the preceding discussion, we have 
    \begin{align*}B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{D^3}(T^3)\simeq \mathrm{Fr}(T^3)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}(T^3)&\simeq (T^3\times \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{R}))/\!\!/ (\mathbb{T}^3\rtimes \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z}))\\ &\cong\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z}).\end{align*}
    To see that the latter is homotopy finite, recall that there is a fiber bundle $\mathrm{O}(3)\hookrightarrow\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{R})\rightarrow \mathcal{Q}_3$, where $\mathcal{Q}_3$ is the space of positive definite $3\times3$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}$. By a result of Soul\'e \cite{Soule78}, $\mathcal{Q}_3$ admits a $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$-equivariant deformation retraction onto a cell complex $X_3\subset \mathcal{Q}_3$ on which the action of $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ is cocompact.  Lifting this deformation retraction to $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{R})$, we find a subspace $\widetilde{X}_3\subset \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{R})$ on which the action of $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ is free, properly discontinuous and cocompact.

By , the identity component Aff_0(M) equals Isom_0(M)cong prod_b SO(2) for any flat metric on M, where b is the rank of the center of pi. Moreover, Aff(M)/Aff_0(M)cong Out(pi). The center of pi is trivial, hence Aff(M)cong Out(pi), which is a finite group (see for a correct calculation of Out(pi)). Moreover, by Corollary and Waldhausen's theorem, this implies that Aff(M)hookrightarrow Diff(M) is a homotopy equivalence. By a result of Zieschang--Zimmermann , for any flat manifold M and any finite subgroup FleqAff(M) there exists a flat metric on M realising F by isometries. Let $M=M_{HW}$ and $\pi=\pi_1(M_{HW})$. Recall that $M$ admits a flat metric, and let $\mathrm{Aff}(M)$ denote the group of affine diffeomorphisms of $M$.  By \cite[Theorem 1,  p474]{CharlapVasquez}, the identity component $\mathrm{Aff}_0(M)$ equals $\mathrm{Isom}_0(M)\cong \prod_b \mathrm{SO}(2)$ for any flat metric on $M$, where $b$ is the rank of the center of $\pi$. Moreover, $\mathrm{Aff}(M)/\mathrm{Aff}_0(M)\cong \mathrm{Out}(\pi)$. The center of $\pi$ is trivial, hence $\mathrm{Aff}(M)\cong \mathrm{Out}(\pi)$, which is a finite group \cite[Example 1]{CharlapVasquez} (see \cite{ZimmermannHW} for a correct calculation of $\mathrm{Out}(\pi)$). Moreover, by Corollary \ref{cor:Diff0-list} and Waldhausen's theorem, this implies that $\mathrm{Aff}(M)\hookrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}(M)$ is a homotopy equivalence. 
    
    By a result of Zieschang--Zimmermann \cite[Satz 3.17]{ZieschangZimmermann}, for any flat manifold $M$ and any finite subgroup $F\leq\mathrm{Aff}(M)$ there exists a flat metric on $M$ realising $F$ by isometries.  Applying this to $\mathrm{Out}(\pi)$ itself, we find a flat metric on $M$ such that $\mathrm{Isom}(M)\cong \mathrm{Aff}(M)\simeq \mathrm{Diff}(M)$. Applying Lemma \ref{lem:Riemannian-Finite-Quotient} completes the proof.

Let $\mathrm{Inn}(G_A)$ denote the group of inner automorphisms.
    Observe that $\mathbb{Z}^2$ injects into $\mathrm{Aut}(G_A)$ as the subgroup $\langle \ell_v \mid v\in \mathbb{Z}^2\rangle$, where $\ell_v$ acts trivially on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and sends $t\mapsto vt$. Now let $\varphi\in \mathrm{Aut}(G_A)$ be any automorphism. By Lemma \ref{lem:Characteristic-Abelian}, $\varphi$ induces $\overline{\varphi}\colon\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ and $\varphi'\colon \mathbb{Z}^2\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}^2$. Since $\overline{\varphi}(t)=t^{\pm1}$, we may assume after composing with $\ell_v$ that $\varphi(t)=t^{\pm1}$. Represent $\varphi'$ by the matrix $B$ with respect to the generators $x,y$. From the presentation in Equation (\ref{eqn:Torus-bundle}), we see that:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item if $\varphi(t)=t$ then $B$ satisfies $BAB^{-1}=A$.
        \item If $\varphi(t)=t^{-1}$ then $B$ satisfies $BAB^{-1}=A^{-1}$.
    \end{enumerate} Conversely, any $B$ satisfying $(1)$ or $(2)$ induces an automorphism of $G_A$ ($t$ gets inverted according to whether $B$ satisfies $(1)$ or $(2)$). The collection of $B\in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ satisfying $(1)$ or $(2)$ is exactly $N_A$. 

    Thus, $N_A$ injects into $\mathrm{Aut}(G_A)$, and $\langle \ell_v\rangle\cap N_A=1$ since $\langle \ell_v\rangle$ acts as the identity on $\mathbb{Z}^2\leq G_A$ but $N_A$ does not.  Moreover, $N_A$ normalises $\langle \ell_v\rangle$ since $B\ell_vB^{-1}=\ell_{Bv}$ for every $B\in N_A$. Hence $\mathrm{Aut}(G_A)= \langle \ell_v\rangle\rtimes N_A$. On the other hand, conjugation by $v\in \mathbb{Z}^2$ acts trivially on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and sends $t\mapsto vtv^{-1}=v(tv^{-1}t^{-1})t=((I-A)v) t$, while conjugation by $t$ acts trivially on $t$ and by $A$ on $\mathbb{Z}^2.$ Therefore
    $\langle \ell_v\rangle\cap \mathrm{Inn}(G_A)= \langle\ell_{(I-A)v}\mid v\in \mathbb{Z}^2\rangle\cong (I-A)\cdot\mathbb{Z}^2$ while $N_A\cap \mathrm{Inn}(G_A)=\langle A\rangle$.  We conclude that $\mathrm{Out}(G_A)\cong (\mathbb{Z}^2/(I-A)\cdot \mathbb{Z}^2)\rtimes (N_A/\langle A\rangle)=F_A\rtimes \overline{N}_A=I_A$ as desired.

Let $\rho\colon M_A\rightarrow S^1$ be the bundle projection. 
    Write $G_A=\pi_1(M_A)=\mathbb{Z}^2\langle x,y\rangle\rtimes_A \mathbb{Z}\langle t\rangle$. Combining Corollary \ref{cor:Diff0-list} part (1), which states that $\mathrm{Diff}_0(M_A)\simeq *$, with Waldhausen's theorem \cite{Waldhausen68} that $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(M_A)\cong \mathrm{Out}(G_A)$, we conclude that $\mathrm{Diff}(M_A)\rightarrow \mathrm{Out}(G_A)$ is a homotopy equivalence.  We will show that $\mathrm{Isom}(M_A)\rightarrow \mathrm{Out}(G_A)$ is an isomorphism. 

   
    By Lemma \ref{lem:Sol-Outer-Automorphism}, $\mathrm{Out}(G_A)\cong I_A = (F_A\rtimes N_A)/\langle A\rangle$. Recall that $I_A$ is finite. We claim $I_A$ can be realised as a finite group of diffeomorphisms of $M_A$, \emph{i.e.}~we construct a splitting of $\mathrm{Diff}(M_A)\rightarrow \mathrm{Out}(G_A)$. Let $\smash{\widetilde{M}_A}\to M_A$ be the regular cover of induced by $\rho_*\colon G_A\to \mathbb{Z}$. Then $\smash{\widetilde{M}_A\cong T^2\times \mathbb{R}}$ and projection onto $\mathbb{R}$ is the lift $\tilde{\rho}$ of $\rho$. 
    Recall that $F_A$ is the group of fixed points of $A$ acting on $T^2$. For any $f\in F_A$ and $v\in T^2$, we have $A(v+f)=Av+f$.  Hence acting trivially on $\mathbb{R}$ and translating of each fiber of $\tilde{\rho}$ by $f$ gives a well-defined diffeomorphism of $\smash{\widetilde{M}_A}$ that commutes with the deck group. Any $B\in N_A$ acts on $T^2$ as a linear map in the standard way, and on $\mathbb{R}$ via the action of $N_A$ on the axis $\gamma\subset \mathbb{H}^2$. The action of $N_A$ normalises the translations $F_A$ so we obtain an action of $F_A\rtimes N_A$ on $\smash{\widetilde{M}_A}$.  Since $F_A\rtimes N_A$ normalises $A$, this action normalises the deck group $\langle A\rangle$ action hence descends to an action of $I_A$ on the quotient $M_A$. Thus we have constructed our splitting and $\mathrm{Out}(G_A)$ acts on $M_A$ by diffeomorphisms. By a result of Meeks--Scott \cite[Theorem 8.2]{Meeks-Scott}, finite group actions on $\mathrm{Sol}$ manifolds preserve the geometric structure. As $I_A$ is finite, $\mathrm{Out}(G_A)$ can be realised on $M_A$ by isometries in the $\mathrm{Sol}$-metric. This implies $\mathrm{Isom}(M_A)\rightarrow \mathrm{Out}(G_A)$ is onto.

    For injectivity, let $\phi\in \mathrm{Isom}(M_A)$ and suppose that $\phi_*\in \mathrm{Out}(G_A)$ is trivial.  Lift $\phi$ to $\smash{\widetilde{\phi}}\colon \mathrm{Sol}\rightarrow \mathrm{Sol}.$ We can choose $\smash{\widetilde{\phi}}$ so that $g\circ \smash{\widetilde{\phi}}=\smash{\widetilde{\phi}}\circ g$ for all $g\in G_A,$ which implies that $\smash{\widetilde{\phi}}$ centralises $G_A$. Since $G_A\cap \mathbb{R}^2$ is a lattice and no element of $D_8$ commutes with an entire lattice in $\mathbb{R}^2$, we must have  $\smash{\widetilde{\phi}}\in \mathrm{Isom}_0(\mathrm{Sol})\cong \mathrm{Sol}$. But the centraliser of any element of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is $\mathbb{R}^2$, while the centraliser of any element projecting nontrivially to $\mathbb{R}$ is the one 1-parameter subgroup containing it.  Since $G_A$ contains elements of both types, its centraliser is trivial.  Thus $\smash{\widetilde{\phi}}$ is the identity, and it follows that $\mathrm{Isom}(M_A)\cong \mathrm{Out}(G_A)$. We conclude that $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{D^3}(M_A)$ is  homotopy finite by \cref{lem:Riemannian-Finite-Quotient}.

Moreover, without loss of generality it suffices to check finiteness of B\!Diff_F^Gamma(M) only for those subgroups Gamma that are contained in the image of \[ pi_0Diff_F(M) longrightarrow pi_0Diff(partial M). \] Since this map factors through pi_0Diff(M), if pi_0Diff_F(M) or pi_0Diff(M) is finite, to show hereditary finiteness it suffices to check the case where Gamma is the entire group.     \[

The main theorem of \cite{HatcherMcCullough} states that $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ is homotopy equivalent to an aspherical finite CW complex.
    In the hyperbolic case $\pi_0 \mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ is a finitely generated free abelian group \cite[Proposition 3.2]{HatcherMcCullough}, so any $\pi_0 \mathrm{Diff}_F^\Gamma(M)$ must also be a finitely generated free abelian group and hence must have a finite classifying space.

    In the case of a Seifert-fibered manifold $\varphi\colon M \to S$ the authors argue  \cite[p108]{HatcherMcCullough} that $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ must have a finite classifying space. During this proof, they construct an intermediate group $G\leq \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ and prove that $G$ has finite classifying space, using only that $\pi_0 \mathrm{Diff}_\partial(M) \leq G$. Therefore their proof applies to $\pi_0 \mathrm{Diff}_F^\Gamma(M)$ for any $\Gamma\le\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(\partial M)$.\qedhere

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{prop:cut-along-sub}
    Let $M$, $F\subset \partial M$, $T\subset \interior{M}$, and $2T\subset \partial (M\smash{\mid} T)$ be as above. 
    Suppose that 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[$(\dagger_0)$]
        there is a component $N_0 \subset M \smash{\mid} T$ such that $N_0 \cap F \neq \emptyset$ and $(N_0, N_0 \cap F)$ is hereditarily finite.
        \item[$(\dagger)$]
        For every other component $N \subset M \smash{\mid} T$ and any non-empty union of components $\emptyset \neq F' \subset \partial N$ containing $N \cap F$, $(N, F')$ is hereditarily finite.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F^{\Gamma}(M, T)$ is homotopy finite for all $\Gamma \le \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(\partial M)$.
    In particular, if $T \subset M$ is canonical, then $(M, F)$ is hereditarily finite.

nodes.statement: The boundary 2T created when cutting M along T is diffeomorphic to two copies of T. In this proof it will be helpful to utilise this and hence we write 2T as T^+ sqcup T^-. (This decomposition into T^+ and T^- is non-canonical and depends on a coorientation of T that we choose arbitrarily.) Hence partial (M smashmid T) = partial M sqcup T^+ sqcup T^-. We proceed by induction over the number of connected components of M smashmid T, starting with the case where M smashmid T is connected, so N_0 = M smashmid T. There is a canonical injective group homomorphism \[ Diff(T) hookrightarrow Diff(T^+ sqcup T^-), varphi mapsto varphi sqcup varphi \] and we define the space of matchings M_T as the coset space Diff(T^+ sqcup T^-)/Diff(T). We have M_T congcoprod_mu_T prod_A in pi_0(T) Diff(A) where mu_T is the finite set of matchings of pi_0(T) (such that matched components are diffeomorphic) and the product runs over all connected components A subset T. Given a matching in mu_T, the product measures the difference between diffeomorphisms on each matched pair of manifolds: there is one such pair for each Ain pi_0(T). In particular, the connected components of M_T are homotopy finite because Diff_0(A) is either SO(3), S^1 times S^1, or a point, depending on the genus of A. The group Diff_F(M smashmid T) acts on M_T via the group homomorphism \[ Diff_F(M smashmid T, 2T) longrightarrow Diff(T^+ sqcup T^-) \] given by restricting to the boundary. Using crefthm:boundary-locally-retractile one can show that M_T is Diff_F(M smashmid T, 2T) locally retractile. The stabiliser of this action is the subgroup of Diff_F(M smashmid T, 2T) consisting of those diffeomorphism that can be glued to a homeomorphism of M. Because the space of collars is contractible (crefthm:contractible-collars), this stabiliser is equivalent to the smaller subgroup of those diffeomorphisms that can be glued to a diffeomorphism of M and this group is isomorphic to Diff_F(M, T). By creflem:orbit-stabiliser-transitive we obtain a homotopy fiber sequence \[ X longrightarrow B\!Diff_F(M, T) longrightarrow B\!Diff_F(M smashmid T, 2T) \] where X subset M_T is the orbit of the basepoint of M_T under the action of B\!Diff_F(M smashmid T, 2T). In fact, we would like to study the smaller group Diff_F^Gamma(Msmashmid T, 2T) for some Gamma le pi_0Diff(partial M). Let Gamma' le pi_0Diff(partial (M smashmid T)) be the subgroup defined as the image of the composite map \[ Diff_F^Gamma(M, T) to Diff_F(M smashmid T) to pi_0 Diff(partial (M smashmid T)). \] This in particular ensures that elements of Diff_F^Gamma'(M smashmid T) preserve 2T subseteq partial (M smashmid T) setwise. Then Diff_F^Gamma(M, T) to Diff_F^Gamma'(M smashmid T) hits all components. So if we let X' subset M_T be the orbit of the base point under the Diff_F^Gamma'(M smashmid T)-action, then X' is connected and as it is a connected component of M_T, it is homotopy finite. Now we apply creflem:orbit-stabiliser-transitive again to get the homotopy fiber sequence \[ X' longrightarrow B\!Diff_F^Gamma(M, T) longrightarrow B\!Diff_F^Gamma'(M smashmid T). \] We have already argued that X' is homotopy finite, and the base is homotopy finite by assumption (dagger_0) (with N_0=Msmashmid T). Therefore the total space is homotopy finite, which proves the base of the induction. Now suppose that M smashmid T has n connected components and that the proposition holds for manifolds T'subset interiorM' such that M'smashmid T' has n' connected components and n'<n. From (dagger_0) there exists a component N_0 subset M smashmid T, which by assumption satisfies that F_0 = partial N cap F is non-empty. We can decompose T = T_0 sqcup T_1 sqcup T_2 where T_i subset T is the union of those connected components that contribute i boundary components to N_0. Let N be the image of N_0 under the map Msmashmid T to M that glues 2T back together. (So T_2 subset interiorN, T_1 subset partial N, and T_0 subset M setminus interiorN.) Then there is a fiber sequence \[ Diff_(F setminus F_0) sqcup N(M, T_0) longrightarrow Diff_F(M, T) xrightarrow\;r\; Diff_F_0(N, T_2). \] Given Gamma le pi_0Diff(partial M) we can choose Gamma' le pi_0Diff(partial N) such that r(Diff_F^Gamma(M, T)) is precisely smashDiff_F_0^Gamma'(N, T_2), so that we get a homotopy fiber sequence \[ B\!Diff_(F setminus F_0) sqcup N^Gamma(M, T_0) longrightarrow B\!Diff_F^Gamma(M, T) xrightarrow\;r\; B\!Diff_F_0^Gamma'(N, T_2). \] The base is homotopy finite by the base of the induction, as N smashmid T_2 is connected. The fiber is equivalent to \[ B\!Diff_(F setminus F_0) sqcup T_1^Gamma''(M setminus interiorN, T_0) \] where Gamma'' le pi_0Diff(partial (M setminus interiorN)) is chosen by restricting Gamma. The manifold (M setminus interiorN)smashmid T_0 has strictly fewer connected components than Msmashmid T by construction, so by the induction hypothesis this space is homotopy finite. (Note that because we introduce new boundary components coming from T_1 that must be fixed, we need the stronger statement (dagger) to ensure that this new manifold still satisfies (dagger_0).) Consequently, by creflem:fiber-sequence-finite the above homotopy fiber sequence shows that B\!Diff_F^Gamma(M, T) is homotopy finite, concluding the proof.

The boundary $2T$ created when cutting $M$ along $T$ is diffeomorphic to two copies of $T$. In this proof it will be helpful to utilise this and hence we write $2T$ as $T^+ \sqcup T^-$.
    (This decomposition into $T^+$ and $T^-$ is non-canonical and depends on a coorientation of $T$ that we choose arbitrarily.)
    Hence $\partial (M \smash{\mid} T) = \partial M \sqcup T^+ \sqcup T^-$.

    We proceed by induction over the number of connected components of $M \smash{\mid} T$, starting with the case where $M \smash{\mid} T$ is connected, so $N_0 = M \smash{\mid} T$.
    There is a canonical injective group homomorphism
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}(T) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}(T^+ \sqcup T^-), \qquad
        \varphi \mapsto \varphi \sqcup \varphi
    \]
    and we define the space of matchings $\mathcal{M}_{T}$ as the coset space $\mathrm{Diff}(T^+ \sqcup T^-)/\mathrm{Diff}(T)$. We have  $$\mathcal{M}_{T} \cong\coprod_{\mu_T} \prod_{A \in \pi_0(T)} \mathrm{Diff}(A)$$ where $\mu_T$ is the finite set of matchings of $\pi_0(T)$ (such that matched components are diffeomorphic) and the product runs over all connected components $A \subset T$. Given a matching in $\mu_T$, the product measures the difference between diffeomorphisms on each matched pair of manifolds: there is one such pair for each $A\in \pi_0(T)$. 
    In particular, the connected components of $\mathcal{M}_{T}$ are homotopy finite because $\mathrm{Diff}_0(A)$ is either $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, $S^1 \times S^1$, or a point, depending on the genus of $A$.
    The group $\mathrm{Diff}_F(M \smash{\mid} T)$ acts on $\mathcal{M}_T$ via the group homomorphism
    \[  
        \mathrm{Diff}_F(M \smash{\mid} T, 2T) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}(T^+ \sqcup T^-)
    \]
    given by restricting to the boundary.
    Using \cref{thm:boundary-locally-retractile} one can show that $\mathcal{M}_T$ is $\mathrm{Diff}_F(M \smash{\mid} T, 2T)$ locally retractile.
    The stabiliser of this action is the subgroup of $\mathrm{Diff}_F(M \smash{\mid} T, 2T)$ consisting of those diffeomorphism that can be glued to a homeomorphism of $M$.
    Because the space of collars is contractible (\cref{thm:contractible-collars}), this stabiliser is equivalent to the smaller subgroup of those diffeomorphisms that can be glued to a diffeomorphism of $M$ and this group is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Diff}_F(M, T)$.
    By \cref{lem:orbit-stabiliser-transitive} we obtain a homotopy fiber sequence
    \[
        X \longrightarrow B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M, T) \longrightarrow B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M \smash{\mid} T, 2T)
    \]
    where $X \subset \mathcal{M}_{T}$ is the orbit of the basepoint of $\mathcal{M}_{T}$ under the action of $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M \smash{\mid} T, 2T)$.
    In fact, we would like to study the smaller group $\mathrm{Diff}_F^\Gamma(M\smash{\mid} T, 2T)$ for some $\Gamma \le \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(\partial M)$.
    Let $\Gamma' \le \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(\partial (M \smash{\mid} T))$ be the subgroup defined as the image of the composite map
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}_F^\Gamma(M, T) \to \mathrm{Diff}_F(M \smash{\mid} T) \to \pi_0 \mathrm{Diff}(\partial (M \smash{\mid} T)).
    \]
    This in particular ensures that elements of $\mathrm{Diff}_F^{\Gamma'}(M \smash{\mid} T)$ preserve $2T \subseteq \partial (M \smash{\mid} T)$ setwise.
    Then $\mathrm{Diff}_F^\Gamma(M, T) \to \mathrm{Diff}_F^{\Gamma'}(M \smash{\mid} T)$ hits all components.
    So if we let $X' \subset \mathcal{M}_{T}$ be the orbit of the base point under the $\mathrm{Diff}_F^{\Gamma'}(M \smash{\mid} T)$-action, then $X'$ is connected and as it is a connected component of $\mathcal{M}_{T}$, it is homotopy finite.
    Now we apply \cref{lem:orbit-stabiliser-transitive} again to get the homotopy fiber sequence
    \[
        X' \longrightarrow B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F^{\Gamma}(M, T) \longrightarrow B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F^{\Gamma'}(M \smash{\mid} T).
    \]
    We have already argued that $X'$ is homotopy finite, and the base is homotopy finite by assumption $(\dagger_0)$ (with $N_0=M\smash{\mid} T$).
    Therefore the total space is homotopy finite, which proves the base of the induction.

    Now suppose that $M \smash{\mid} T$ has $n$ connected components and that the proposition holds for manifolds $T'\subset \interior{M}'$ such that $M'\smash{\mid} T'$ has $n'$ connected components and $n'<n$.
    From $(\dagger_0)$ there exists a component $N_0 \subset M \smash{\mid} T$, which by assumption satisfies that $F_0 = \partial N \cap F$ is non-empty. 

    We can decompose $T = T_0 \sqcup T_1 \sqcup T_2$ where $T_i \subset T$ is the union of those connected components that contribute $i$ boundary components to $N_0$.
    Let $N$ be the image of $N_0$ under the map $M\smash{\mid} T \to M$ that glues $2T$ back together.
    (So $T_2 \subset \interior{N}$, $T_1 \subset \partial N$, and $T_0 \subset M \setminus \interior{N}$.)
    Then there is a fiber sequence
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}_{(F \setminus F_0) \sqcup N}(M, T_0) \longrightarrow
        \mathrm{Diff}_F(M, T) \xrightarrow{\;r\;}
        \mathrm{Diff}_{F_0}(N, T_2).
    \]
    Given $\Gamma \le \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(\partial M)$ we can choose $\Gamma' \le \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(\partial N)$ such that 
    $r(\mathrm{Diff}_F^\Gamma(M, T))$ is precisely $\smash{\mathrm{Diff}_{F_0}^{\Gamma'}(N, T_2)}$, so that we get a homotopy fiber sequence
    \[
        B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{(F \setminus F_0) \sqcup N}^{\Gamma}(M, T_0) \longrightarrow
        B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F^\Gamma(M, T) \xrightarrow{\;r\;}
        B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{F_0}^{\Gamma'}(N, T_2).
    \]
    The base is homotopy finite by the base of the induction, as $N \smash{\mid} T_2$ is connected.
    The fiber is equivalent to 
    \[
        B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{(F \setminus F_0) \sqcup T_1}^{\Gamma''}(M \setminus \interior{N}, T_0)
    \]
    where $\Gamma'' \le \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(\partial (M \setminus \interior{N}))$ is chosen by restricting $\Gamma$.
    
    The manifold $(M \setminus \interior{N})\smash{\mid} T_0$ has strictly fewer connected components than $M\smash{\mid} T$ by construction, so by the induction hypothesis this space is homotopy finite.
    (Note that because we introduce new boundary components coming from $T_1$ that must be fixed, we need the stronger statement $(\dagger)$ to ensure that this new manifold still satisfies $(\dagger_0)$.)
    Consequently, by \cref{lem:fiber-sequence-finite} the above homotopy fiber sequence shows that $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F^\Gamma(M, T)$ is homotopy finite, concluding the proof.
