So if we let X' subset M_T be the orbit of the base point under the Diff_F^Gamma'(M smashmid T)-action, then X' is connected and as it is a connected component of M_T, it is homotopy finite. Now we apply creflem:orbit-stabiliser-transitive again to get the homotopy fiber sequence \[ X' longrightarrow B\!Diff_F^Gamma(M, T) longrightarrow B\!Diff_F^Gamma'(M smashmid T). \] We have already argued that X' is homotopy finite, and the base is homotopy finite by assumption (dagger_0) (with N_0=Msmashmid T). Therefore the total space is homotopy finite, which proves the base of the induction. Now suppose that M smashmid T has n connected components and that the proposition holds for manifolds T'subset interiorM' such that M'smashmid T' has n' connected components and n'<n. From (dagger_0) there exists a component N_0 subset M smashmid T, which by assumption satisfies that F_0 = partial N cap F is non-empty. We can decompose T = T_0 sqcup T_1 sqcup T_2 where T_i subset T is the union of those connected components that contribute i boundary components to N_0. Let N be the image of N_0 under the map Msmashmid T to M that glues 2T back together. (So T_2 subset interiorN, T_1 subset partial N, and T_0 subset M setminus interiorN.) Then there is a fiber sequence \[ Diff_(F setminus F_0) sqcup N(M, T_0) longrightarrow Diff_F(M, T) xrightarrow\;r\; Diff_F_0(N, T_2). \] Given Gamma le pi_0Diff(partial M) we can choose Gamma' le pi_0Diff(partial N) such that r(Diff_F^Gamma(M, T)) is precisely smashDiff_F_0^Gamma'(N, T_2), so that we get a homotopy fiber sequence \[ B\!Diff_(F setminus F_0) sqcup N^Gamma(M, T_0) longrightarrow B\!Diff_F^Gamma(M, T) xrightarrow\;r\; B\!Diff_F_0^Gamma'(N, T_2). \] The base is homotopy finite by the base of the induction, as N smashmid T_2 is connected. The fiber is equivalent to \[ B\!Diff_(F setminus F_0) sqcup T_1^Gamma''(M setminus interiorN, T_0) \] where Gamma'' le pi_0Diff(partial (M setminus interiorN)) is chosen by restricting Gamma. The manifold (M setminus interiorN)smashmid T_0 has strictly fewer connected components than Msmashmid T by construction, so by the induction hypothesis this space is homotopy finite. (Note that because we introduce new boundary components coming from T_1 that must be fixed, we need the stronger statement (dagger) to ensure that this new manifold still satisfies (dagger_0).) Consequently, by creflem:fiber-sequence-finite the above homotopy fiber sequence shows that B\!Diff_F^Gamma(M, T) is homotopy finite, concluding the proof.

nodes.statement: The Teichm\"uller space of marked, flat 2-tori can be identified with the upper half plane H^2, equipped with its natural hyperbolic metric. GL_2(Z) acts properly discontinuously on H^2 by isometries, altering the marking by a change of basis. Since H^2 is complete, simply connected, and nonpositively curved, any finite subgroup Gamma< GL_2(Z) has a global fixed point. This corresponds to a flat metric on T^2 which realises Gamma by isometries. Since the identity component of Diff(T^2) is homotopy equivalent to T^2, the group of translations, Diff^Gamma(T^2) is homotopy equivalent to a subgroup T^2rtimes Gamma that acts freely on Fr^perp(T^2). Lemma now completes the proof.

\label{prop:cut-along-tori}
    Let $M$ be a compact connected $3$-manifold and $T \subset \interior{M}$ a union of tori.
    Assume that $T$ is canonical, i.e.~the inclusion $\mathrm{Diff}(M, T) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}(M)$ is an equivalence.
    Suppose that any connected component $N$ of $M \smash{\mid} T$ satisfies:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item 
        $(N \setminus \interior{D}^3, S^2)$ is hereditarily finite.
        \item
        For any non-empty union of boundary components $F \subset (2T \cap \partial N)$,
        $(N, F)$ is hereditarily finite. 
        \item The image of $\mathrm{Diff}(M, T) \to \pi_0(\mathrm{Diff}(T))$ is a finite group.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then $(M \setminus \interior{D}^3, S^2)$ is hereditarily finite.

nodes.statement: Let Fr_3(T) subset Fr(M) denote the subspace of those framed points based in T. An element of Fr_3(T) is a tuple of a point p in T and a frame for T_p(T) oplus R, so in particular Fr_3(T) is different from Fr(T) . Recall that 2T = partial (M smashmid T) setminus partial M. This is the co-orientation double cover of T and we can picture this as being obtained from T by translating it infinitesimally in both normal directions. Since T is two-sided (i.e.~co-oriented in M) we know that 2T cong T sqcup T, but this identification is not canonical as it requires choosing a coorientation for each component, which we do not do in this proof as the action of Diff(M,T) will not necessarily preserve the decomposition. We can re-glue M as (Msmashmid T) cup_2T T, and similarly we can write the frame bundle on M as a pushout \[ Fr(M) = Fr(M smashmid T) cup_Fr_3(2T) Fr_3(T). \] This is in fact a homotopy pushout because submanifold inclusions are cofibrations. It is moreover equivariant for the group Diff^Gamma(M, T), so by creflem:homotopy-orbits-functor we obtain the following homotopy pushout square. \[ Fr_3(2T)/\!\!/ Diff^Gamma(M, T) ar[r] ar[d] & Fr(M smashmid T)/\!\!/ Diff^Gamma(M, T) ar[d] \\ Fr_3(T)/\!\!/ Diff^Gamma(M, T) ar[r] & Fr(M)/\!\!/ Diff^Gamma(M, T) \] The bottom right term is Fr(M) /\!\!/ Diff^Gamma(M, T) simeq Fr(M) /\!\!/ Diff^Gamma(M) simeq Diff_D^3^Gamma(M), so to prove the claim it will suffice to show that the three other terms in the square are homotopy finite. We begin with the top right term Fr(M smashmid T) /\!\!/ Diff^Gamma(M, T). We can equivalently replace Fr(M smashmid T) by Emb(D^3, (M smashmid T)^circ). The space Emb(D^3, (Msmashmid T)^circ) is Diff_0((M smashmid T)^circ)-locally retractile by combining crefthm:emb-retractile, with creflem:locally-retractile(3) and (4). We conclude it is locally retractile for the action of the larger group Diff^Gamma(M, T) by creflem:locally-retractile(4). We may then apply the homotopy orbit stabiliser lemma (creflem:orbit-stabiliser-v2) to compute \[ Emb(D^3,(M smashmid T)^circ)/\!\!/ Diff^Gamma(M, T) simeq coprod_[icolon D^3 hookrightarrow (M smashmid T)^circ] BDiff_i(D^3)^Gamma(M, T). \] Here the coproduct runs over the set of orbits of the action of Diff^Gamma(M, T) on pi_0Emb(D^3, (M smashmid T)^circ), which is finite because pi_0Fr(M smashmid T) is finite. In each orbit we pick an embedded icolon D^3 hookrightarrow (M smashmid T)^circ as a representative and the corresponding term in the coproduct is the classifying space of the stabiliser group Diff_i(D^3)^Gamma(M, T). This is equivalent to B\!Diff_partial D^3^Gamma(M setminus interiorD^3, T), which is homotopy finite by applying crefprop:cut-along-sub to T subset M setminus interiorD^3 with F=S^2. (Condition (dagger_0) is satisfied for the component where we removed the disk by (1) and condition (dagger) is satisfied by (2).) We still have to deal with the two left hand terms in the homotopy pushout square, but the left vertical map in the square is a double-covering, so it suffices to show finiteness of Fr_3(T) /\!\!/ Diff^Gamma(M,T). Choose at each point p in T a normal vector up to sign pm xi_p smoothly depending on p. This is a contractible space of choices, so the subgroup Diff_pm xi^Gamma(M, T) subset Diff^Gamma(M, T) of those diffeomorphism varphi satisfying Dvarphi(xi_p) = pm xi_varphi(p) is equivalent to the entire group. We then have a fiber sequence \[ Fr_pmxi(T) longrightarrow Fr_3(T) longrightarrow (R^3setminus 0)/pm \] where the fibration sends a framed point (p in T, thetacolon R^3 cong T_pM) to theta^-1(pm xi_p). The fiber Fr_pmxi(T) is the subspace of those framed points on T whose first vector is xi_p or -xi_p. There is a homotopy equivalence Fr(2T) simeq Fr_pmxi(T) defined by extending the 2-framing to a 3-framing by adding pm xi_p with the sign depending on the coorientation. Taking homotopy orbits via creflem:fiberseq/fiberseq applied to the short exact fiber sequence Diff_pmxi^Gamma(M, T)to Diff_pmxi^Gamma(M, T)to *, we get a homotopy fiber sequence \[ Fr(2T)/\!\!/ Diff_pmxi^Gamma(M, T) longrightarrow Fr_3(T)/\!\!/ Diff_pmxi^Gamma(M, T) longrightarrow (R^3setminus 0)/pm \] where the base is equivalent to the finite CW complex RP^2. By the homotopy orbit stabiliser lemma (creflem:orbit-stabiliser-v2), the fiber has finitely many connected components (since pi_0(Fr(2T)) is finite) each of which is equivalent to \[ B\!Diff_D^2^Gamma, +(M, T) \] where we fix some 2-disk in T as well as its co-orientation in M. (Together with the fixed 2-disk, the latter is equivalent to being orientation-preserving.) Now there is a homotopy fiber sequence \[ B\!Diff_T_0^Gamma,+(M, T) longrightarrow B\!Diff_D^2^Gamma, +(M, T) longrightarrow B\!Diff_D^2^Gamma'(T_0) \] where T_0 subset T is the connected component containing the disk and Gamma' < pi_0(Diff(T_0)) consists of those isotopy classes that can be extended to a diffeomorphism in Diff^Gamma,+(M, T). The base is homotopy finite by creflem:2torus-finite because Gamma' is finite by assumption (3). The fiber is equivalent to B\!Diff_2T_0^Gamma(Msmashmid T_0, T setminus T_0) where we write 2T_0 subset partial(M smashmid T_0) for the two new tori created by cutting along T_0. This space is homotopy finite by crefprop:cut-along-sub applied to T setminus T_0 subset M smashmid T_0 with F = T_0. (M smashmid T_0 might not be connected, but because the components cannot be permuted, we can apply crefprop:cut-along-sub to each component individually.) Applying creflem:fiber-sequence-finite completes the proof.

Let $\mathrm{Fr}_3(T) \subset \mathrm{Fr}(M)$ denote the subspace of those framed points based in $T$.
    An element of $\mathrm{Fr}_3(T)$ is a tuple of a point $p \in T$ and a frame for $T_p(T) \oplus \mathbb{R}$, so in particular $\mathrm{Fr}_3(T)$ is different from $\mathrm{Fr}(T)$ .

    Recall that $2T = \partial (M \smash{\mid} T) \setminus \partial M$.
    This is the co-orientation double cover of $T$ and
    we can picture this as being obtained from $T$ by translating it infinitesimally in both normal directions.
    Since $T$ is two-sided (\emph{i.e.}~co-oriented in $M$) we know that $2T \cong T \sqcup T$, but this identification is not canonical as it requires choosing a coorientation for each component, which we do not do in this proof as the action of $\mathrm{Diff}(M,T)$ will not necessarily preserve the decomposition.

    We can re-glue $M$ as $(M\smash{\mid} T) \cup_{2T} T$, and similarly we can write the frame bundle on $M$ as a pushout 
    \[
        \mathrm{Fr}(M) = \mathrm{Fr}(M \smash{\mid} T) \cup_{\mathrm{Fr}_3(2T)} \mathrm{Fr}_3(T).
    \]
    This is in fact a homotopy pushout because submanifold inclusions are cofibrations.
    It is moreover equivariant for the group $\mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M, T)$, so by \cref{lem:homotopy-orbits-functor} we obtain the following homotopy pushout square.
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
        \mathrm{Fr}_3(2T)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M, T) \ar[r] \ar[d] & 
        \mathrm{Fr}(M \smash{\mid} T)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M, T) \ar[d] \\
        \mathrm{Fr}_3(T)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M, T) \ar[r] & 
        \mathrm{Fr}(M)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M, T)
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    The bottom right term is $\mathrm{Fr}(M) /\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M, T) \simeq \mathrm{Fr}(M) /\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M) \simeq \mathrm{Diff}_{D^3}^\Gamma(M)$, so to prove the claim it will suffice to show that the three other terms in the square are homotopy finite.

    We begin with the top right term $\mathrm{Fr}(M \smash{\mid} T) /\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M, T)$.
    We can equivalently replace $\mathrm{Fr}(M \smash{\mid} T)$ by $\mathrm{Emb}(D^3, (M \smash{\mid} T)^\circ)$.
    The space $\mathrm{Emb}(D^3, (M\smash{\mid} T)^\circ)$ is $\mathrm{Diff}_0((M \smash{\mid} T)^\circ)$-locally retractile by combining \cref{thm:emb-retractile}, with \cref{lem:locally-retractile}(3) and (4). We conclude it is locally retractile for the action of the larger group $\mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M, T)$ by \cref{lem:locally-retractile}(4).
    We may then apply the homotopy orbit stabiliser lemma (\cref{lem:orbit-stabiliser-v2}) to compute
    \[
        \mathrm{Emb}(D^3,(M \smash{\mid} T)^\circ)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M, T) 
        \simeq \coprod_{[i\colon D^3 \hookrightarrow (M \smash{\mid} T)^\circ]} B\mathrm{Diff}_{i(D^3)}^\Gamma(M, T).
    \]
    Here the coproduct runs over the set of orbits of the action of $\mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M, T)$ on $\pi_0\mathrm{Emb}(D^3, (M \smash{\mid} T)^\circ)$, which is finite because $\pi_0\mathrm{Fr}(M \smash{\mid} T)$ is finite.
    In each orbit we pick an embedded $i\colon D^3 \hookrightarrow (M \smash{\mid} T)^\circ$ as a representative and the corresponding term in the coproduct is the classifying space of the stabiliser group  $\mathrm{Diff}_{i(D^3)}^\Gamma(M, T)$.
    This is equivalent to $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{\partial D^3}^\Gamma(M \setminus \interior{D}^3, T)$, which is homotopy finite by applying \cref{prop:cut-along-sub} to $T \subset M \setminus \interior{D}^3$ with $F=S^2$.
    (Condition $(\dagger_0)$ is satisfied for the component where we removed the disk by $(1)$ and condition $(\dagger)$ is satisfied by $(2)$.) 
    

    We still have to deal with the two left hand terms in the homotopy pushout square, 
    but the left vertical map in the square is a double-covering, so it suffices to show finiteness of $\mathrm{Fr}_3(T) /\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M,T)$.
    Choose at each point $p \in T$ a normal vector up to sign $\pm \xi_p$ smoothly depending on $p$.
    This is a contractible space of choices, so the subgroup $\mathrm{Diff}_{\pm \xi}^\Gamma(M, T) \subset \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M, T)$ of those diffeomorphism $\varphi$ satisfying $D\varphi(\xi_p) = \pm \xi_{\varphi(p)}$ is equivalent to the entire group.
    We then have a fiber sequence
    \[
        \mathrm{Fr}_{\pm\xi}(T) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Fr}_3(T) \longrightarrow (\mathbb{R}^3\setminus 0)/\pm
    \]
    where the fibration sends a framed point $(p \in T, \theta\colon \mathbb{R}^3 \cong T_pM)$ to $\theta^{-1}(\pm \xi_p)$.

We have subgroup inclusions Z/p le SO(2) le Diff(S^1) such that the generator of Z/p is sent to the diffeomorphism that rotates by zeta_p = e^2pi i/p. We let Diff(S^1)^Z/p denote the fixed points of the conjugation action by zeta, or in other words the centraliser of Z/p. There is a group homomorphism \[ alphacolon Diff(S^1)^Z/p longrightarrow Diff^v(M), f longmapsto left( [x, y] mapsto [f(x), y]right) \] which is well defined because [zeta_p x, zeta_p^q y] mapsto [f(zeta_p x), zeta_p^q y] = [zeta_p f(x), zeta_p^q y]. A Z/p-equivariant diffeomorphism f in Diff(S^1)^Z/p induces a diffeomorphism barf in Diff(S^1/(Z/p)), and alpha(f) is the diffeomorphism of M that is barf on the central fiber and f on the non-singular fibers. In particular, we can define a one-sided inverse to alpha by restricting a vertical diffeomorphism g in Diff^v(M) to any non-singular fiber, and therefore alpha is an embedding. The image of alpha consists of those g that induce the same diffeomorphism on all non-singular fibers. We can construct a deformation retraction to this subgroup by setting \[ Hcolon Diff^v(S^1 times D^2) times (0,1] longrightarrow Diff^v(S^1 times D^2), g longmapsto left( [x,y] mapsto [g|_S^1([x,ty]), y]right) \] and then continuously extending this to [0,1]. Alternatively H(g, t)([x,y]) can be obtained by multiplying the second coordinate of g([x,ty]) by tfrac1t. This H defines a homotopy such that H(-,1) is the identity and H(-,0) is a retraction onto the subspace that is the image of Diff(S^1)^Z/p. We will construct a Z/p-equivariant deformation retraction from Diff(S^1) to O(2). Any orientation-preserving diffeomorphism f in Diff^+(S^1) can be represented by a Z-equivariant tildef in Diff^+(R) and two such lifts represent the same element of Diff^+(S^1) if they differ by a constant integer. We define the average offset of tildef as a = int_0^1 tildef(x) - x\; dx and then construct the affine isotopy \[ tildef_t(x) := (1-t) cdot tildef(x) + t cdot (x + a). \] This is still Z-equivariant and the equivalence class [tildef_t] in Diff^+(S^1) is independent of the choice of tildef. Therefore hcolon [0,1] times Diff^+(S^1) to Diff^+(S^1) given by h(t,f)= [tildef_t] defines a deformation retraction of Diff^+(S^1) onto SO(2), which is equivariant for the Z/p-action given by conjugation with zeta. (Indeed, the deformation retraction is equivariant for the conjugation action by SO(2) because it comes from an R-equivariant deformation retraction on Diff(R).) The orientation-reversing case is treated similarly. In summary, Diff(S^1) deformation retracts Z/p-equivariantly to O(2) and passing to fixed points we see that Diff(S^1)^Z/p simeq Diff^v(S^1 times D^2) is equivalent to the space of Z/p-fixed points on O(2). For p=1 this is O(2). For p=2 it is also O(2) because zeta_2 = -1 is central in O(2). For pge 3 (and 0<q<p) it is SO(2) because this is the centraliser of zeta in O(2).

We may assume that the fibering is of the standard form $\varphi_{(p,q)} \colon M = (S^1 \times D^2)/(\mathbb{Z}/p) \to D^2/(\mathbb{Z}/p)$ described above.
    We have subgroup inclusions $\mathbb{Z}/p \le \mathrm{SO}(2) \le \mathrm{Diff}(S^1)$ such that the generator of $\mathbb{Z}/p$ is sent to the diffeomorphism that rotates by $\zeta_p = e^{2\pi i/p}$.
    We let $\mathrm{Diff}(S^1)^{\mathbb{Z}/p}$ denote the fixed points of the conjugation action by $\zeta$, or in other words the centraliser of $\mathbb{Z}/p$.
    There is a group homomorphism
    \[
        \alpha\colon \mathrm{Diff}(S^1)^{\mathbb{Z}/p} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}^v(M), \qquad
        f \longmapsto \left( [x, y] \mapsto [f(x), y]\right)
    \]
    which is well defined because $[\zeta_p x, \zeta_p^q y] \mapsto [f(\zeta_p x), \zeta_p^q y] = [\zeta_p f(x), \zeta_p^q y]$.
    A $\mathbb{Z}/p$-equivariant diffeomorphism $f \in \mathrm{Diff}(S^1)^{\mathbb{Z}/p}$ induces a diffeomorphism $\bar{f} \in \mathrm{Diff}(S^1/(\mathbb{Z}/p))$, 
    and $\alpha(f)$ is the diffeomorphism of $M$ that is $\bar{f}$ on the central fiber and $f$ on the non-singular fibers.
    In particular, we can define a one-sided inverse to $\alpha$ by restricting a vertical diffeomorphism $g \in \mathrm{Diff}^v(M)$ to any non-singular fiber, and therefore $\alpha$ is an embedding.
    The image of $\alpha$ consists of those $g$ that induce the same diffeomorphism on all non-singular fibers.
    We can construct a deformation retraction to this subgroup by setting
    \[
        H\colon \mathrm{Diff}^v(S^1 \times D^2) \times (0,1] \longrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}^v(S^1 \times D^2), \qquad
        g \longmapsto \left( [x,y] \mapsto [g|_{S^1}([x,ty]), y]\right)
    \]
    and then continuously extending this to $[0,1]$.
    Alternatively $H(g, t)([x,y])$ can be obtained by multiplying the second coordinate of $g([x,ty])$ by $\tfrac{1}{t}$.
    This $H$ defines a homotopy such that $H(-,1)$ is the identity and $H(-,0)$ is a retraction onto the subspace that is the image of $\mathrm{Diff}(S^1)^{\mathbb{Z}/p}$.
    
    We will construct a $\mathbb{Z}/p$-equivariant deformation retraction from $\mathrm{Diff}(S^1)$ to $\mathrm{O}(2)$.
    Any orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f \in \mathrm{Diff}^+(S^1)$ can be represented by a $\mathbb{Z}$-equivariant $\tilde{f} \in \mathrm{Diff}^+(\mathbb{R})$ and two such lifts represent the same element of $\mathrm{Diff}^+(S^1)$ if they differ by a constant integer.
    We define the average offset of $\tilde{f}$ as $a = \int_0^1 \tilde{f}(x) - x\; \mathrm{dx}$ and then construct the affine isotopy
    \[
        \tilde{f}_t(x) := (1-t) \cdot \tilde{f}(x) + t \cdot (x + a).
    \]
    This is still $\mathbb{Z}$-equivariant and the equivalence class $[\tilde{f}_t] \in \mathrm{Diff}^+(S^1)$ is independent of the choice of $\tilde{f}$.
    Therefore $h\colon [0,1] \times \mathrm{Diff}^+(S^1) \to \mathrm{Diff}^+(S^1)$ given by $h(t,f)= [\tilde{f}_t]$ defines a deformation retraction of $\mathrm{Diff}^+(S^1)$ onto $\mathrm{SO}(2)$, which is equivariant for the $\mathbb{Z}/p$-action given by conjugation with $\zeta$.
    (Indeed, the deformation retraction is equivariant for the conjugation action by $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ because it comes from an $\mathbb{R}$-equivariant deformation retraction on $\mathrm{Diff}(\mathbb{R})$.)
    The orientation-reversing case is treated similarly.

    In summary, $\mathrm{Diff}(S^1)$ deformation retracts $\mathbb{Z}/p$-equivariantly to $\mathrm{O}(2)$ and passing to fixed points we see that $\mathrm{Diff}(S^1)^{\mathbb{Z}/p} \simeq \mathrm{Diff}^v(S^1 \times D^2)$ is equivalent to the space of $\mathbb{Z}/p$-fixed points on $\mathrm{O}(2)$.
    For $p=1$ this is $\mathrm{O}(2)$.
    For $p=2$ it is also $\mathrm{O}(2)$ because $\zeta_2 = -1$ is central in $\mathrm{O}(2)$.
    For $p\ge 3$ (and $0<q<p$) it is $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ because this is the centraliser of $\zeta$ in $\mathrm{O}(2)$.

By \cite[Corollary 3.8(ii)]{HKMR12} there is a locally trivial fiber sequence
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}_\partial^v(M) \longrightarrow 
        \mathrm{Diff}^v(M) \longrightarrow 
        \mathrm{Diff}^v(\partial M).
    \]
    Since the boundary $\partial M \to \partial D$ of the Seifert fibering is always diffeomorphic to the trivial fibration $S^1 \times S^1 \to S^1$,
    a diffeomorphism in $\mathrm{Diff}^v(\partial M)$ is simply a smooth $S^1$-family in $\mathrm{Diff}(S^1)$.
    Therefore $\mathrm{Diff}^v(\partial M) \simeq \mathrm{Map}(S^1, \mathrm{O}(2)) \simeq \mathbb{Z} \times \mathrm{O}(2)$.
    Combining this with \cref{lem:Diffv-solid-torus} we see that the map $\mathrm{Diff}^v(M) \to \mathrm{Diff}^v(\partial M)$ is equivalent to either $\mathrm{SO}(2) \to \mathbb{Z} \times \mathrm{O}(2)$ or $\mathrm{O}(2) \to \mathbb{Z} \times \mathrm{O}(2)$.
    In either case it is a homotopy equivalence onto the components it hits and hence its fiber $\mathrm{Diff}_\partial^v(M)$ is contractible, proving (\ref{it:Diffv-contractible}).

    Claim (\ref{it:Difff-contractible}) is now a consequence of combining (\ref{it:Diffv-contractible}) with the fiber sequence
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}_\partial^v(M) \to 
        \mathrm{Diff}_\partial^f(M) \to 
        \mathrm{Diff}_\partial(D)
    \]
     from \cite[Theorem 3.9]{HKMR12}. The base and fiber are contractible, and hence so is the total space.

    To show (\ref{it:MCGf}), note that by \cref{lem:Diffv-solid-torus} $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}^v(M)$ is trivial if $p\ge 3$ and $\{[\mathrm{id}], [\alpha]\}$ if $p \le 2$.
    Inspecting the long exact sequence of the fiber sequence (again from \cite[Theorem 3.9]{HKMR12})
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}^v(M) \to 
        \mathrm{Diff}^f(M) \to 
        \mathrm{Diff}(D)
    \]
    we see that because $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(D) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ generated by the (complex) reflection, $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}^f(M)$ is indeed generated by $\beta$ (and $\alpha$ if $p \le 2$), proving (\ref{it:MCGf}).

    For (\ref{it:extend}), we first note that 
    the map $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}^f(\partial M) \to \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$,
    which records the action on first homology, is injective and its image consists of those matrices that preserve the homology class of the fiber up to sign.
    If $\varphi \in \mathrm{Diff}^f(\partial M)$ can be extended to a diffeomorphism of $M$,
    then $\varphi$ it also preserves the homology class of the meridian (which bounds in $M$) up to sign.
    A basis for $H_1(\partial M) \cong \mathbb{Z}^2$ is given by the fiber $(p,q)$ and the meridian $(0,1)$.
    Then we have that $\varphi_*(p,q) = \pm (p,q)$ and $\varphi_*(0,1) = \pm(0,1)$.
    If $(p,q) = (1,0)$ or $(2,1)$, then there are four elements of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ satisfying these equations and if $p \ge 3$, then only $\mathrm{id}$ and $-\mathrm{id}$ satisfy them.

    In any of these cases, $\varphi$ can be extended to a fiberwise diffeomorphism of $M$.

The restriction mapping $\mathrm{Diff}(S^1\times D^2)\rightarrow \mathrm{Diff}(T^2)$ is a locally trivial fibration over the components of $\mathrm{Diff}(T^2)$ in its image with fiber $\mathrm{Diff}_\partial(S^1\times D^2)$. The latter is contractible by \cite{Hatcher76, Ivanov76}, hence $\mathrm{Diff}_0(S^1\times D^2)\simeq\mathrm{Diff}_0(T^2)\simeq \mathrm{SO}(2)\times \mathrm{SO}(2)$. Since the meridian is the unique simple closed curve on $T^2$ which bounds in $S^1\times D^2$, and $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(T^2)\cong \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$, the image of $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(S^1\times D^2)$ lies the in the subgroup $\mathrm{GL}_2^{\langle e_1\rangle}(\mathbb{Z})$ which preserves the subgroup $\langle e_1\rangle$:
\[\mathrm{GL}_2^{\langle e_1\rangle}(\mathbb{Z})=\left\{
        \begin{pmatrix}
            \pm 1 & * \\
            0 & \pm 1
        \end{pmatrix}
        \right\}.\] 
Conversely, the group $\mathrm{Aff}(T^2)\cong\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\ltimes (\mathrm{SO}(2)\times \mathrm{SO}(2))$ of affine diffeomorphisms acts on $T^2$, and the subgroup $\mathrm{GL}_2^{\langle e_1\rangle}(\mathbb{Z})\ltimes(\mathrm{SO}(2)\times \mathrm{SO}(2)) $ extends to $S^1\times D^2$ as a group of affine diffeomorphisms, when equipped with its standard Euclidean structure. Thus, the inclusion $\mathrm{GL}_2^{\langle e_1\rangle}(\mathbb{Z})\ltimes\mathrm{SO}(2)^2 \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}(S^1\times D^2)$ is a homotopy equivalence.


    We need to show that $\mathrm{Fr}(S^1 \times D^2) /\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(S^1 \times D^2)$ is homotopy finite for all $\Gamma < \mathrm{GL}_2^{\langle e_1\rangle}(\mathbb{Z})$. By the above diescussion, $\mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(S^1 \times D^2)\simeq \Gamma \ltimes \mathrm{SO}(2)^2$.
    The frame bundle satisfies
    \( \mathrm{Fr}(S^1 \times D^2) \simeq S^1\times D^2 \times \mathrm{O}(3) \simeq S^1 \times \mathrm{O}(3) \).
    The map $p\colon \mathrm{Fr}(S^1 \times D^2) \to \mathbb{R}\mathrm{P}^2$ that records the line spanned by the first frame vector at the point $S^1 \times \{0\}$ is invariant under the action of $\mathrm{GL}_2^{\langle e_1\rangle}(\mathbb{Z}) \ltimes \mathrm{SO}(2)^2$.
    The fiber of $p$ is equivalent to $S^1 \times \mathrm{O}(2) \times \mathbb{Z}/2$, so we have a homotopy fiber sequence
    \[
        (S^1 \times \mathrm{O}(2) \times \mathbb{Z}/2) /\!\!/ (\Gamma \ltimes \mathrm{SO}(2)^2)
        \longrightarrow \mathrm{Fr}(S^1 \times D^2) /\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(S^1 \times D^2)
        \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}\mathrm{P}^2.
    \]
    The base is finite so we concentrate on the fiber.
    To compute the homotopy orbits we first take the quotient by the identity component $\mathrm{SO}(2)^2$, which acts freely on the first two factors, and get 
    \[
        (S^1 \times \mathrm{O}(2) \times \mathbb{Z}/2) /\!\!/ \mathrm{SO}(2)^2 \simeq(S^1 \times \mathrm{O}(2) \times \mathbb{Z}/2) / \mathrm{SO}(2)^2
        \simeq \mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2.
    \]
    The remaining action of the mapping class group $\mathrm{GL}_2^{\langle e_1\rangle}(\mathbb{Z})$ is given by the projection $\theta\colon \mathrm{GL}_2^{\langle e_1\rangle}(\mathbb{Z}) = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2 \ltimes \mathbb{Z} \to (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$.
    In particular, the subgroup $\mathbb{Z}$ acts trivially, and $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ acts in the canonical way.
    For any $\Gamma < \mathrm{GL}_2^{\langle e_1\rangle}(\mathbb{Z})$ we have a fiber sequence
    \[
        B(\Gamma \cap \ker(\theta)) \longrightarrow
        (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2 /\!\!/ \Gamma \longrightarrow
        (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2/\theta(\Gamma).
    \]
    The base is a finite set.
    The kernel $\ker(\theta)$ is $\mathbb{Z}$, so $\Gamma \cap \ker(\theta)$ is either infinite cyclic or $0$ -- either way its classifying space is homotopy finite. Applying \cref{lem:fiber-sequence-finite} completes the proof.

nodes.statement: If S is a disk then F = partial M=partial (S^1times D^2) and Diff_partial^v(S^1 times D^2) simeq * by creflem:solid-torus-facts(1). We can now induct on the complexity of the surface. Let alpha be an arc in S connecting two points of varphi(F) such that either S setminus alpha is connected and has lower complexity, or is disconnected and both pieces have lower complexity. Let A = varphi^-1(alpha) be the annulus that is the preimage of alpha. By there is a fiber sequence \[ Diff^v_F cup A(M) longrightarrow Diff_F^v(M) longrightarrow Diff_F cap A^v(A) \] The fibering of the annulus A to alpha is necessarily trivial, so the base of the fiber sequence can be identified with Diff_partial^v(S^1 times I), an element of which can be thought of as a smooth loop in the space Diff(S^1). Hence it is equivalent to the discrete group \[ Diff_F cap A^v(A) simeq Omega Diff(S^1) simeq Z. \] The fiber of the fiber sequence is equivalent to Diff_F cup 2A^v(M smashmid A) where we cut along A and fix the new boundary created by A. By induction hypothesis this is equivalent to Z^n for some n. Inspecting the long exact sequence we see that the components of Diff_F^v(M) are contractible and that there is an exact sequence \[ 1 to Z^n to pi_0Diff_F^v(M) to Z, \] so Diff_F^v(M) is equivalent to either Z^n or Z^n+1.

If $S$ is a disk then $F = \partial M=\partial (S^1\times D^2)$ and $\mathrm{Diff}_\partial^v(S^1 \times D^2) \simeq *$ by \cref{lem:solid-torus-facts}(1).
    We can now induct on the complexity of the surface.
    Let $\alpha$ be an arc in $S$ connecting two points of $\varphi(F)$ such that either $S \setminus \alpha$ is connected and has lower complexity, or is disconnected and both pieces have lower complexity.
    Let $A = \varphi^{-1}(\alpha)$ be the annulus that is the preimage of $\alpha$.
    By \cite[Corollary 3.8(ii)]{HKMR12} there is a fiber sequence
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}^v_{F \cup A}(M) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}_F^v(M) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}_{F \cap A}^v(A)
    \]
    The fibering of the annulus $A \to \alpha$ is necessarily trivial, so the base of the fiber sequence can be identified with
    $\mathrm{Diff}_\partial^v(S^1 \times I)$,
    an element of which can be thought of as a smooth loop in the space $\mathrm{Diff}(S^1)$.
    Hence it is equivalent to the discrete group
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}_{F \cap A}^v(A) \simeq \Omega \mathrm{Diff}(S^1) \simeq \mathbb{Z}.
    \]
    The fiber of the fiber sequence is equivalent to $\mathrm{Diff}_{F \cup 2A}^v(M \smash{\mid} A)$ where we cut along $A$ and fix the new boundary created by $A$.
    By induction hypothesis this is equivalent to $\mathbb{Z}^n$ for some $n$.
    Inspecting the long exact sequence we see that the components of $\mathrm{Diff}_F^v(M)$ are contractible and that there is an exact sequence
    \[
        1 \to \mathbb{Z}^n \to \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}_F^v(M) \to \mathbb{Z},
    \]
    so $\mathrm{Diff}_F^v(M)$ is equivalent to either $\mathbb{Z}^n$ or $\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$.

When acting by Diff^f(M) on the frame bundle, the fiber-direction of the tangent space is always preserved. Therefore the map Fr(M) & longrightarrow RP^2 \\ (p, alpha colon R^3 cong T_pM) &longmapsto alpha^-1(ker d_pvarphi) subset R^3 is invariant under the action of Diff^f(M). Let Fr'(M) subset Fr(M) denote the fiber of this map, i.e.~those framings where the first vector lies in the tangent space of the fiber. By creflem:fiberseq/fiberseq we have a homotopy fiber sequence \[ Fr'(M)/\!\!/ Diff^f,Gamma(M) longrightarrow Fr(M)/\!\!/ Diff^f,Gamma(M) longrightarrow RP^2 \] and we show that the total space is homotopy finite. Since the base is a finite CW complex, by creflem:fiber-sequence-finite it will suffice to consider the fiber. The map Fr'(M) to Fr(S) defined by forgetting the first vector of the framing and then applying varphi and dvarphi is a fibration, and its fiber Fr''(S^1) is equivalent to the frame bundle of S^1. This fiber sequence Fr''(S^1) longrightarrow Fr'(M) longrightarrow Fr(S) is equivariant for the principal short exact sequence Diff^v,Gamma(M) longrightarrow Diff^f,Gamma(M) longrightarrow Diff'(S). that we obtain by restricting crefeqn:fix fiber to account for Gamma. Here Diff'(S) le Diff(S) is defined as the image of Diff^f,Gamma(M), and this is a finite index subgroup by creflem:SF-finite-index. The action of Diff^v(M) on Fr(S^1) has either one or two orbits, depending on whether there is a bundle-preserving diffeomorphism that reverses the orientation of the fiber. Either way the map \[ Diff^v(M) longrightarrow Diff(S^1) xrightarrow\ simeq\ Fr(S^1), \] which first restricts the diffeomorphism to a fiber and then evaluates it and its derivative at a point, is a fiber bundle by (furthermore the second map is a trivial Serre fibration). Let $\varphi \colon M \to S$ be the non-singular Seifert fibering such that $\mathrm{Diff}^f(M) \simeq \mathrm{Diff}(M)$.
    We need to show that for all $\Gamma < \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(\partial M)$ the space
    \[
        B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{D^3}^\Gamma(M) \simeq \mathrm{Fr}(M)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^\Gamma(M) \simeq \mathrm{Fr}(M) /\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^{f, \Gamma}(M)
    \]
    is homotopy finite.
    When acting by $\mathrm{Diff}^f(M)$ on the frame bundle, the fiber-direction of the tangent space is always preserved.
    Therefore the map
    \begin{align*}
        \mathrm{Fr}(M) & \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}\mathrm{P}^2 \\ 
        (p, \alpha \colon \mathbb{R}^3 \cong T_pM) &\longmapsto \alpha^{-1}(\ker d_p\varphi) \subset \mathbb{R}^3
    \end{align*}
    is invariant under the action of $\mathrm{Diff}^f(M)$.
    Let $\mathrm{Fr}'(M) \subset \mathrm{Fr}(M)$ denote the fiber of this map, \emph{i.e.}~those framings where the first vector lies in the tangent space of the fiber. By \cref{lem:fiberseq/fiberseq} we have a homotopy fiber sequence
    \[
        \mathrm{Fr}'(M)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^{f,\Gamma}(M) \longrightarrow
        \mathrm{Fr}(M)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^{f,\Gamma}(M) \longrightarrow
        \mathbb{R}\mathrm{P}^2
    \]
    and we show that the total space is homotopy finite.
    Since the base is a finite CW complex, by \cref{lem:fiber-sequence-finite} it will suffice to consider the fiber.
    The map $\mathrm{Fr}'(M) \to \mathrm{Fr}(S)$ defined by forgetting the first vector of the framing and then applying $\varphi$ and $d\varphi$ is a fibration, and its fiber $\mathrm{Fr}''(S^1)$ is equivalent to the frame bundle of $S^1$.
    This fiber sequence 
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn:Fr-fibration}
        \mathrm{Fr}''(S^1) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Fr}'(M) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Fr}(S)
    \end{equation}
    is equivariant for the principal short exact sequence
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn:Diff-fibration}
        \mathrm{Diff}^{v,\Gamma}(M) \longrightarrow
        \mathrm{Diff}^{f,\Gamma}(M) \longrightarrow
        \mathrm{Diff}'(S).
    \end{equation}
    that we obtain by restricting \cref{eqn:fix fiber} to account for $\Gamma$.
    Here $\mathrm{Diff}'(S) \le \mathrm{Diff}(S)$ is defined as the image of $\mathrm{Diff}^{f,\Gamma}(M)$, and this is a finite index subgroup by \cref{lem:SF-finite-index}.
    
    Taking the quotient of (\ref{eqn:Fr-fibration}) by (\ref{eqn:Diff-fibration}), \cref{lem:fiberseq/fiberseq} yields a homotopy fiber sequence
    \[
        \mathrm{Fr}(S^1)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^{v,\Gamma}(M) \longrightarrow
        \mathrm{Fr}'(M)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^{f,\Gamma}(M) \longrightarrow
        \mathrm{Fr}(S)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}'(S).
    \]
    The base is equivalent to $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{D^2}'(S)$, which is a finite cover of $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{D^2}(S)$, which in turn is homotopy finite by Lemma \ref{lem:Surface-Fix-Disk-finite}, so it suffices to consider the fiber.
    
    The action of $\mathrm{Diff}^v(M)$ on $\mathrm{Fr}(S^1)$ has either one or two orbits, depending on whether there is a bundle-preserving diffeomorphism that reverses the orientation of the fiber.
    Either way the map
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}^v(M) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}(S^1) \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ } \mathrm{Fr}(S^1),
    \]
    which first restricts the diffeomorphism to a fiber and then evaluates it and its derivative at a point, is a fiber bundle by \cite[Corollary 3.8.(ii)]{HKMR12} (furthermore the second map is a trivial Serre fibration). Hence the homotopy orbit-stabiliser lemma (\cref{lem:orbit-stabiliser-v2}) tells us
    \[
        \mathrm{Fr}(S^1)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^{v, \Gamma}(M) \simeq \mathrm{Diff}(S^1)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}^{v, \Gamma}(M) \simeq B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{S^1}^{v, \Gamma}(M) \times \begin{cases}
            * \\
            * \sqcup * 
        \end{cases}
    \]
    where the case distinction depends on whether there exists fiberwise orientation-reversing diffeomorphism.
    For $U\subset M$ a vertical tubular neighbourhood of $S^1$ we have 
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}_{S^1}^v(M) \simeq \mathrm{Diff}_U^v(M) \simeq \mathrm{Diff}_{\partial U}^v(M\setminus \interior{U}) \simeq \mathbb{Z}^n
    \]
    where the last equivalence comes from \cref{lem:Diff_S1^v-v2}.
    Hence the group $\mathrm{Diff}_{S^1}^{v,\Gamma}(M)$ must be equivalent to some subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}^n$, so it also is finite rank free abelian and its classifying space is homotopy finite.

nodes.statement: Let M be a Haken Seifert-fibered 3-manifold with a fiber-rigid fibering varphicolon M to S. Let U be a vertical tubular neighbourhood of the singular fibers, and let T := partial U be its boundary. Then M setminus interiorU to varphi(M setminus interiorU) is fiber-rigid, Diff(M, U) = Diff(M, T), and the inclusions \[ Diff(M, T) hookrightarrow Diff(M) and Diff^f(M, T)hookrightarrow Diff(M,T) \] are both equivalences. $M$ cannot be a solid torus, because the solid torus only has flexible fiberings. 
    Because $M$ is Haken we know either $S$ is not a sphere or it is a sphere and there are at least three singular fibers.
    Therefore $S \setminus \varphi(U)^\circ$ is neither an annulus, nor a disk. 
    By \cref{rem:most-non-singular-are-rigid} the only flexible Seifert-fibered manifolds with boundary are the solid torus and $T^2 \times I$, which only fiber over the disk and the annulus.
    Hence $M \setminus \interior{U} \to S \setminus \varphi(U)^\circ$ is a non-singular fiber-rigid Haken Seifert-fibering.
    Moreover, $U$ is a disjoint union of solid tori and $M \setminus \interior{U}$ is connected and not a solid torus, so any diffeomorphism preserving $T$ must also preserve $U$, \emph{i.e.}~$\mathrm{Diff}(M,T)\simeq \mathrm{Diff}(M,T)$.


    Since the diffeomorphism group of the base orbifold already preserves the singularities, it is equivalent to the subgroup $\mathrm{Diff}(S, \varphi(U)) < \mathrm{Diff}(S)$ where we additionally preserve small disks around the singularities.
    Pulling this equivalence back along the fibration $\mathrm{Diff}^f(M) \to \mathrm{Diff}(S)$ from \cref{eqn:fix fiber} we get that $\mathrm{Diff}^f(M, T) \simeq \mathrm{Diff}^f(M)$.
    This equivalence fits in a square of subgroup inclusions
    
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
    	{\mathrm{Diff}^f(M, T)} & {\mathrm{Diff}^f(M)} \\
    	{\mathrm{Diff}(M, T)} & {\mathrm{Diff}(M)}
    	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
    	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
    	\arrow["\simeq", from=1-1, to=1-2]
    	\arrow["\simeq", from=1-2, to=2-2]
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    and to show that the bottom map is an equivalence as claimed it will suffice to check our final claim: that the left hand map is an equivalence.
    The left map in turn fits into a map of homotopy fiber sequences:

\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathrm{Diff}_\partial^f(U)} & {\mathrm{Diff}^f(M, T)} & {\mathrm{Diff}^f(M \setminus \interior{U})} \\
	{\mathrm{Diff}_\partial(U)} & {\mathrm{Diff}(M, T)} & {\mathrm{Diff}(M \setminus \interior{U})}
	\arrow["\simeq"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\simeq", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
    The right vertical map is an equivalence because $M\setminus \interior{U}$ is fiber-rigid.
    The left vertical map is an equivalence because $\mathrm{Diff}_\partial(S^1 \times D^2)$ is contractible by \cite{Hatcher76, Ivanov76} and $\mathrm{Diff}_\partial^f(U)$ is contractible by \cref{lem:solid-torus-facts}.(2).
    From the long exact sequence of homotopy groups it follows that the middle map is an isomorphism on $\pi_n$ for $n\ge1$ and an injection on $\pi_0$.
    To see that it is also surjective on $\pi_0$ let $\xi\in \mathrm{Diff}(M, T)$.
    Because $M\setminus \interior{U}$ is fiber-rigid we can isotope $\xi_{|M \setminus \interior{U}}$ to a fiber-preserving diffeomorphism, and we may extend this isotopy to all of $M$ while preserving $T$ as a subset. Denote the result of this isotopy by $\varphi\in \mathrm{Diff}(M, T)$.
    Now $\varphi_{|U}$ is fiber-preserving on $\partial U$ and hence, by \cref{lem:solid-torus-facts}.(3), there is a $\psi \in \mathrm{Diff}^f(U)$ with $\varphi_{|\partial U} = \psi_{|\partial U}$.
    We have $\varphi_{|U} \circ \psi^{-1} \in \mathrm{Diff}_\partial(U) \simeq *$, so there must be an isotopy from $\varphi_{|U}$ to $\psi$ relative to $\partial U$.
    This shows that $\xi$ is isotopic to an element of $\mathrm{Diff}^f(M, T)$.

nodes.statement: If M is non-singular apply creflem:Haken-SF-Nonsingular. Otherwise, pick a vertical tubular neighbourhood U of the singular fibers as in creflem:singular-fiber-canonical; then T := partial U is a canonical submanifold by that lemma. We apply crefprop:cut-along-tori. The second condition follows from crefthm:HM-hereditary. For the third condition, creflem:singular-fiber-canonical also shows that Diff(M, T) simeq Diff^f(M, T) and so the image of Diff(M, T) to pi_0 Diff(T) is finite because each of the tori bounds a fibered solid torus and pi_0 Diff^f( U ) is finite by creflem:solid-torus-facts(4). Hence crefprop:cut-along-tori reduces the claim to hereditary finiteness for (N setminus interiorD^3, S^2) where N is any connected component of M smashmid T. Most of the components are solid tori and we checked in creflem:solid-torus that ((S^1 times D^2 )setminus interiorD^3, S^2) is hereditarily finite. The remaining connected component is the non-singular piece M setminus interiorU. As observed in creflem:singular-fiber-canonical M setminus interiorU is non-singular Seifert-fibered and still fiber-rigid. As such (M setminus (U sqcup D^3)^circ, S^2) satisfies hereditary finiteness by creflem:Haken-SF-Nonsingular.

nodes.statement: For any union of components R subset T we let Sub_0(R, interiorM) subset Sub(R, interiorM) denote the path-component of the space of those unparametrised embeddings that contain the submanifold R subset interiorM. We will prove that Sub_0(R, interiorM) is contractible by induction on the number of connected components of R subset T. If there is only one torus, then this is Hatcher's theorem . For the induction step, we suppose that Sub_0(R, interiorM) is contractible. We will show that Sub_0(R sqcup A, interiorM) is contractible for some torus A subset T setminus N. We can define a map \[ fcolon Sub_0(R sqcup A, interiorM) to Sub_0(R, interiorM) \] by taking a submanifold V subset interiorM to V setminus B subset interiorM where B subset V is the unique connected component that is isotopic to A subset interiorM. Because we are in the path component Sub_0, we know that there always is such a B, and because no two tori in T are isotopic, it is unique. Therefore, f is well-defined, continuous, and Diff_0(M)-equivariant. But Sub_0(R, interiorM) is Diff_0(M)-locally retractile by crefcor:umb-retractile, so f is a fiber bundle by creflem:locally-retractile(1). We can identify the fiber f^-1([R]) with the identity component of unparametrised embeddings of A into (Msetminus R)^circ. (Indeed, the long exact sequence of the fibration implies that the fiber is connected, as the total space is connected and the base contractible by the induction hypothesis.) Hence we have the fiber sequence \[ Sub_0(A, (M setminus R)^circ) longrightarrow Sub_0(R sqcup A, interiorM) longrightarrow Sub_0(R, interiorM). \] By induction hypothesis both fiber and total space are contractible and we conclude that the total space must also be contractible, completing the induction. To obtain the conclusion about Diff(M, T) we consider the fiber sequence \[ Diff(M, T) longrightarrow Diff(M) longrightarrow Sub(T, interiorM) \] from the discussion after crefcor:umb-retractile. The image of the fibration is exactly the Diff(M)-orbit of the canonical unparametrised embedding T subset interiorM. By the uniqueness of JSJ decompositions we know that for any varphi in Diff(M) we have that varphi(T) is (unparametrised) isotopic to T, so the image of the fibration is the path-component of the base point, i.e.~Sub_0(T, interiorM), which we know to be contractible. Hence the inclusion Diff(M, T) to Diff(M) is an equivalence as claimed.

    Therefore, $f$ is well-defined, continuous, and $\mathrm{Diff}_0(M)$-equivariant.
    But $\mathrm{Sub}_0(R, \interior{M})$ is $\mathrm{Diff}_0(M)$-locally retractile by \cref{cor:umb-retractile}, so $f$ is a fiber bundle by \cref{lem:locally-retractile}(1).
    We can identify the fiber $f^{-1}([R])$ with the identity component of unparametrised embeddings of $A$ into $(M\setminus R)^\circ$.
    (Indeed, the long exact sequence of the fibration implies that the fiber is connected, as the total space is connected and the base contractible by the induction hypothesis.)
    Hence we have the fiber sequence
    \[
        \mathrm{Sub}_0(A, (M \setminus R)^\circ) \longrightarrow 
        \mathrm{Sub}_0(R \sqcup A, \interior{M}) \longrightarrow
        \mathrm{Sub}_0(R, \interior{M}).
    \]
    By induction hypothesis both fiber and total space are contractible and we conclude that the total space must also be contractible, completing the induction.

    To obtain the conclusion about $\mathrm{Diff}(M, T)$ we consider the fiber sequence
    \[
        \mathrm{Diff}(M, T) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Diff}(M) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Sub}(T, \interior{M})
    \]
    from the discussion after \cref{cor:umb-retractile}.
    The image of the fibration is exactly the $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$-orbit of the canonical unparametrised embedding $T \subset \interior{M}$.
    By the uniqueness of JSJ decompositions we know that for any $\varphi \in \mathrm{Diff}(M)$ we have that $\varphi(T)$ is (unparametrised) isotopic to $T$,
    so the image of the fibration is the path-component of the base point, \emph{i.e.}~$\mathrm{Sub}_0(T, \interior{M})$, which we know to be contractible.
    Hence the inclusion $\mathrm{Diff}(M, T) \to \mathrm{Diff}(M)$ is an equivalence as claimed.

nodes.statement: First, we restrict to the finite index subgroup of Diff(M,T) consisting of those diffeomorphisms that fix the dual graph of T. It is enough to show that for this subgroup the lemma holds. To do this, we claim that for each torus T_i subseteq T there are a finite number of mapping classes on T_i that can be extended to an element of Diff(M, T). Let M_i' and M_i'' be the JSJ pieces on either side of T_i (note that M_i' may equal M_i''). First, consider the case where at least one of M_i' or M_i'' is a hyperbolic manifold N. Then, since the dual graph is fixed, the map in question factors through Diff(N, T_i), but we know that pi_0Diff(N) = pi_0 Isom(N) is finite, so the image is finite. If neither of the sides of T_i is hyperbolic, then they must both be Seifert-fibered. Neither side is D^2times S^1 nor T^2times I, hence they are both fiber-rigid by Remark . Let alpha_i' and alpha_i'' in H_1(T_i) be the images of the two fiber curves on T_i. Since M_i'cup_T_iM_i'' is not Seifert-fibered, alpha_i' and alpha_i'' represent linearly independent elements of pi_1(T_i). Any element of Diff(M,T) that fixes the dual graph of T thus maps both alpha_i' and alpha_i'' to themselves or their inverses. As alpha_i' and alpha_i'' are linearly independent, there at most four elements of GL_2(Z)cong pi_0(Diff(T_i)) that satisfy this condition.

We may therefore suppose that~$M$ has non-trivial JSJ decomposition and is not the total space of a $T^2$-bundle over $S^1$. Let $T \subset M$ be the collection of JSJ tori, which is a canonical submanifold by \cref{cor:JSJ-canonical}. \label{lem:finiteness-fixing-balls}
    Suppose that $M$ is a connected 3-manifold and $F \subseteq \partial M$ is a union of connected components of its boundary.

        \simeq B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M \setminus \interior{B}, \partial B) .
    \]

    The group in the fiber is equivalent to $\mathrm{Diff}_\partial(B)$, which is a product of $\mathrm{Diff}_\partial(D^3)$'s, hence  contractible by Hatcher's proof of the Smale conjecture.
    This shows that the fibration is an equivalence, which gives us the second equivalence.

    Both actions are locally retractile, so we can apply \cref{lem:orbit-stabiliser-transitive} to obtain homotopy fiber sequences:
    \begin{align*}
        \mathrm{Sub}(B, M) \longrightarrow
        & B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M, B) \longrightarrow B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M)\\
         \mathrm{Emb}^+(B, M) \longrightarrow
        &B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{F\sqcup B}(M) \longrightarrow B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M). 
    \end{align*}
    Since we assumed that the base spaces are homotopy finite in both cases, it will suffice to argue that the fibers a homotopy finite.
    We pass to considering 
    The space $\mathrm{Emb}(B, M)$ since $\mathrm{Emb}^+(B, M)$ is a union of path components. Then
    $\mathrm{Emb}(B, M) = \mathrm{Emb}(\amalg_k D^3, M)$ is homotopy equivalent to $\mathrm{Conf}_{k}^{\rm fr}(M)$, the space of ordered framed configurations of $M$.

    \[
        \mathrm{Fr}(M \setminus \{p_1, \dots, p_{k-1}\}) \longrightarrow
        \mathrm{Conf}_{k}^{\rm fr}(M) \longrightarrow
        \mathrm{Conf}_{k-1}^{\rm fr}(M \setminus \{p\}) 
    \]
    and the fact that the frame bundle of a punctured version of $M$ is still homotopy finite.

Both actions are locally retractile, so we can apply creflem:orbit-stabiliser-transitive to obtain homotopy fiber sequences: Sub(B, M) longrightarrow & B\!Diff_F(M, B) longrightarrow B\!Diff_F(M)\\ Emb^+(B, M) longrightarrow &B\!Diff_Fsqcup B(M) longrightarrow B\!Diff_F(M). Since we assumed that the base spaces are homotopy finite in both cases, it will suffice to argue that the fibers a homotopy finite. We pass to considering The space Emb(B, M) since Emb^+(B, M) is a union of path components. Then Emb(B, M) = Emb(amalg_k D^3, M) is homotopy equivalent to Conf_k^fr(M), the space of ordered framed configurations of M. This space is homotopy finite, as can be seen by inductively using the homotopy fiber sequence \[ Fr(M setminus \p_1, dots, p_k-1\) longrightarrow Conf_k^fr(M) longrightarrow Conf_k-1^fr(M setminus \p\) \] and the fact that the frame bundle of a punctured version of M is still homotopy finite. The space Sub(B, M) is obtained from Emb(B, M) by taking the quotient with respect to the Diff(B) action. Because Diff(D^3) simeq SO(3), we get that Sub(B, M) is homotopy equivalent to the unordered configuration space of k points in M. This is equivalent to the quotient of the free strata-preserving action of Sigma_k on the Fulton-MacPherson compactification C_k[M] . As such it is itself a compact manifold with corners and hence homotopy finite.

We can write $M = \widehat{M}\setminus \interior{B}$ for $B$ a disjoint union of disks. 
    Decompose $B = B_1 \sqcup B_2$ such that $F \cap \partial B = \partial B_1$
    and write $F_0 = F \cap \partial \scl{M}= F \setminus \partial B_1$.

    There are two cases. 
    If $F_0 \neq \emptyset$ we will reduce to \cref{thm: HatcherMcCullough finiteness} of Hatcher--McCullough \cite{HatcherMcCullough}, who show that $\mathrm{Diff}_{F_0}(\widehat{M})$ is homotopy finite.
    Applying \cref{lem:finiteness-fixing-balls} once, we see that $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{F_0 \sqcup \partial B_1}(\scl{M}\setminus \interior{B}_1)$ is homotopy finite.
    Applying it again we get that
    \[
        B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{F_0 \sqcup \partial B_1}(\scl{M}\setminus \interior{B}, \partial B_2)
        =
        B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{F}(M, \partial B_2)
        = B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M)
    \]
    is homotopy finite.
    Here the first equality holds because $F_0 \sqcup \partial B_1 = F$ and $\widehat{M}\setminus \interior{B} = M$.
    The second equality holds because any diffeomorphism of $M$ must fix $\partial B$ as a subset (because these are the spherical boundaries) and so if it fixes $\partial B_1$ pointwise, it must automatically fix $\partial B_2$ as a subset.

    If $F_0 = \emptyset$, then $  \partial B_1=F \neq \emptyset$ must be non-empty.
    In this case we reduce to \cref{thm:sect4main}.
    Pick some preferred component $D \subset B_1$.
    Then \cref{thm:sect4main} tells us that $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_D(\scl{M})$
    is homotopy finite.
    Applying \cref{lem:finiteness-fixing-balls} twice gives firstly that $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{B_1}(\scl{M})$ is homotopy finite and then that
    \[
        B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{B_1}(\scl{M}\setminus \interior{B}_2, \partial B_2) 
        \simeq B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{\partial B_1}(\scl{M}\setminus \interior{B}, \partial B_2) 
        = B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{\partial B_1}(\scl{M}\setminus \interior{B})
        = B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{F}(M)
    \]
    is also homotopy finite.

nodes.statement: Since M is not prime, every Sigma in Sep^nparallel(M) is non-empty. We can construct a dual graph G_Sigma that has a vertex for each component of M smashmid Sigma and an edge for each sphere in Sigma. Let v be the number of vertices and e the number of edges in this graph. This dual graph must have first Betti number g and therefore it has Euler characteristic v-e = 1-g. Let us say that a vertex is special if it corresponds to a component N subset M smashmid Sigma that contains a prime factor or a boundary sphere of M, and let v_0 be the number of special vertices. Then we have v_0 le n+m, as there are n prime factors and m boundary spheres in M. A vertex is non-special if the manifold obtained from N subset M smashmid Sigma by filling in the boundary spheres coming from 2Sigma is a 3-sphere. Every non-special vertex is at least trivalent: if it was univalent the sphere in Sigma that bounds it would not be essential, and if it was bivalent the two spheres in Sigma that bound it would be parallel. (The two spheres at a bivalent vertex also cannot be the same sphere because M notcong S^1 times S^2.) In summary we have at least three half-edges per non-special vertex and at least one half-edge per special vertex (as M is connected and Sigma non-empty). This yields the inequality 2e ge 3(v-v_0) + v_0. Rewriting, we get 2e ge 3v - 2v_0 ge 3v - 2(n+m). Using the Euler characterisitc equation v-e=1-g from before we get that \[ v le 2(n+m+g-1) qquadand e le 2(n+m) + 3(g-1) \] as claimed.

Since $M$ is not prime, every $\Sigma \in \mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}(M)$ is non-empty.
    We can construct a dual graph $G_\Sigma$ that has a vertex for each component of $M \smash{\mid} \Sigma$ and an edge for each sphere in $\Sigma$.
    Let $v$ be the number of vertices and $e$ the number of edges in this graph.
    This dual graph must have first Betti number $g$ and therefore it has Euler characteristic $v-e = 1-g$.
    Let us say that a vertex is \emph{special} if it corresponds to a component $N \subset M \smash{\mid} \Sigma$ that contains a prime factor or a boundary sphere of $M$, and let $v_0$ be the number of special vertices.
    Then we have $v_0 \le n+m$, as there are $n$ prime factors and $m$ boundary spheres in $M$.
    A vertex is non-special if the manifold obtained from $N \subset M \smash{\mid} \Sigma$ by filling in the boundary spheres coming from $2\Sigma$ is a $3$-sphere.
    Every non-special vertex is at least trivalent:
    if it was univalent the sphere in $\Sigma$ that bounds it would not be essential, 
    and if it was bivalent the two spheres in $\Sigma$ that bound it would be parallel.
    (The two spheres at a bivalent vertex also cannot be the same sphere because $M \not\cong S^1 \times S^2$.)

    Rewriting, we get $2e \ge 3v - 2v_0 \ge 3v - 2(n+m)$.
    Using the Euler characterisitc equation $v-e=1-g$ from before we get that
    \[
        v \le 2(n+m+g-1) 
        \qquad\text{and}\qquad
        e \le 2(n+m) + 3(g-1)
    \]
    as claimed.

nodes.statement: First, note that Sep^nparallel(M)/Diff_F(M) is a discrete topological space and so any two isotopic separating systems lie in the same orbit. This follows because Sep^nparallel(M) is locally Diff_F(M)-retractile or equivalently, by isotopy extension. We now essentially follow the proof of . Recall M decomposes as \[ Mcong left(P_1\#cdots \#P_n \# (S^1times S^2)^\# gright)setminus \amalg_m interiorD^3\ cong P_1\#cdots \#P_n \# (S^1times S^2)^\# g \# (D^3)^\# m. \] We can hence construct M by attaching g 1-handles to S^3, and taking the connected sum with the P_i and with m copies of D^3. Let B = amalg_n+m+2g D^3 subset S^3 be the collection of 3-disks along which we performed these attachments. Now suppose we have some Sigma in Sep^nparallel(M). Then (based on work of Scharlemann) tells us that there is a diffeomorphism varphi in Diff_F(M) (in fact fixing a neighbourhood of the boundary) such that varphi(Sigma) subset M lies entirely in S^3setminus interiorB. Therefore to show the set Sep^nparallel(M)/Diff_F(M) is finite, it will suffice to show that up to isotopy there are finitely many sphere systems (without parallel spheres) in S^3setminus interiorB. This is indeed the case because such isotopy classes are uniquely determined by how they partition the finite set of boundary components. Indeed, since S^3setminus interiorB is simply connected, pi_2(S^3setminus B)cong H_2(S^3setminus interiorB), so homotopy classes of embedded spheres agree with homology classes, which in turn correspond to how they partition partial B. By Laudenbach , homotopic spheres are isotopic. The claim for sphere systems is now straightforward.

First, note that $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}(M)/\mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ is a discrete topological space and so any two isotopic separating systems lie in the same orbit.

    We now essentially follow the proof of \cite[Lemma 2.1]{HatcherMcCullough1990}.
    Recall $M$ decomposes as
    \[
        M\cong \left(P_1\#\cdots \#P_n \# (S^1\times S^2)^{\# g}\right)\setminus \{\amalg_m \interior{D}^3\}
        \cong P_1\#\cdots \#P_n \# (S^1\times S^2)^{\# g} \# (D^3)^{\# m}.
    \]
    We can hence construct $M$ by attaching $g$ $1$-handles to $S^3$, and taking the connected sum with the $P_i$ and with $m$ copies of $D^3$.
    Let $B = \amalg_{n+m+2g} D^3 \subset S^3$ be the collection of $3$-disks along which we performed these attachments.

    Now suppose we have some $\Sigma \in \mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}(M)$. 
    Then \cite[Lemma 2.1]{HatcherMcCullough1990} (based on work of Scharlemann~\cite[Appendix A]{Bonahon-Cobordism}) tells us that there is a diffeomorphism $\varphi \in \mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ (in fact fixing a neighbourhood of the boundary) such that $\varphi(\Sigma) \subset M$ lies entirely in $S^3\setminus \interior{B}$.

\label{prop:finiteness-sphere-system}
    Let $M$ be a compact connected $3$-manifold, $\emptyset \neq F \subseteq \partial M$ a non-empty union of boundary components such that $\partial M \setminus F$ contains only spheres and incompressible tori, and let $\Sigma \in \mathrm{Sep}(M)$ be a separating system.
    Then $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M , \Sigma)$
    is homotopy finite.

nodes.statement: Since partial Mneq emptyset, Mneq S^1times S^2. We know by Theorem~ that the fat geometric realisation \|Sep^nparallel_bullet(M)\| is contractible. Let Sep^nparallel,subset_bullet(M) denote the semi-simplicial space where n-simplices are strict inclusions of separating systems with no parallel spheres. The simplicial space Sep^nparallel_bullet(M) is obtained from Sep^nparallel,subset_bullet(M) by freely adding degeneracies, so by we have an equivalence \|Sep^nparallel_bullet(M)\| simeq \|Sep^nparallel,subset_bullet(M)\|. (Note that \|Sep^nparallel,subset_bullet(M)\| is in fact homeomorphic to the thin geometric realisation |Sep^nparallel_bullet(M)|.) The semi-simplicial space Sep^nparallel,subset_bullet(M) has the advantage that there is a bound on the dimension of the simplices that can appear: if M has m spherical boundary components and sclM is the connected sum of n irreducible prime factors and g copies of (S^1 times S^2), then creflem:bounding-graphs says that each separating system in Sep^nparallel(M) contains at most 2(n+m) + 3(g-1) spheres. Therefore any chain of more than 2(n+m)+3(g-1) inclusions must include an identity, and so Sep^nparallel,subset_i(M) = emptyset for i > 2(n+m)+3(g-1). Diff_F(M) acts on Sep^nparallel,subset_bullet(M) levelwise by postcomposition -- non-parallel spheres are taken to non-parallel spheres under diffeomorphisms of~M. We therefore get an action of Diff_F(M) on \|Sep^nparallel,subset_bullet(M)\| and since \|Sep^nparallel,subset_bullet(M)\| is contractible, the homotopy orbit space of this action is a model for the classifying space: \[ B\!Diff_F(M) simeq \|Sep^nparallel,subset_bullet(M)\|/\!\!/ Diff_F(M) cong \|Sep^nparallel,subset_bullet /\!\!/ Diff_F(M) \|. \] Here we use that (-)/\!\!/ G commutes with fat geometric realisation by creflem:homotopy-orbits-functor. Since there are only simplices up to a certain dimension, it will suffice to prove that for all n the space \[ Sep^nparallel,subset_n(M)/\!\!/Diff_F(M) \] is homotopy finite. To reduce this to the case of n=0 recall from creflem:face-map-is-finite-covering that the last vertex map Sep^nparallel,subset_n(M) to Sep^nparallel(M) is a finite covering. Therefore the map from Sep^nparallel,subset_n(M) /\!\!/ Diff_F(M) to Sep^nparallel(M)/\!\!/ Diff_F(M) is also a finite covering and it will suffice to show that the latter is homotopy finite. By the homotopical orbit stabiliser theorem (creflem:orbit-stabiliser-v2) there is a decomposition \[ Sep^nparallel(M) /\!\!/ Diff_F(M) simeq coprod_[x] B\!Diff_F(M,Sigma) \] where the coproduct runs over a set of representatives of Sep^nparallel(M)/Diff_F(M). Each of the terms in the coproduct is homotopy finite by crefprop:finiteness-sphere-system. Moreover, we showed Sep^nparallel(M)/Diff_F(M) is finite in creflem:finitely-many-graphs-HM. This completes the proof as we have written Sep^nparallel(M)/\!\!/ Diff_F(M) as a finite coproduct of homotopy finite spaces.

Since $\partial M\neq \emptyset$, $M\neq S^1\times S^2$.  We know by Theorem~\ref{thm: sepNP contractible} that the fat geometric realisation $\|\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}_\bullet(M)\|$ is contractible.
Let $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_\bullet(M)$ denote the semi-simplicial space where $n$-simplices are strict inclusions of separating systems with no parallel spheres.
The simplicial space $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}_\bullet(M)$ is obtained from $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_\bullet(M)$ by freely adding degeneracies, 
so by \cite[Lemma 2.6]{EbertRandalWilliams} we have an equivalence
$\|\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}_\bullet(M)\| \simeq \|\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_\bullet(M)\|$.
(Note that $\|\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_\bullet(M)\|$ is in fact homeomorphic to the \emph{thin} geometric realisation $|\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}_\bullet(M)|$.)
The semi-simplicial space $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_\bullet(M)$ has the advantage that there is a bound on the dimension of the simplices that can appear:
if $M$ has $m$ spherical boundary components and $\scl{M}$ is the connected sum of $n$ irreducible prime factors and $g$ copies of $(S^1 \times S^2)$, then \cref{lem:bounding-graphs} says that each separating system in $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}(M)$ contains at most $2(n+m) + 3(g-1)$ spheres. 
Therefore any chain of more than $2(n+m)+3(g-1)$ inclusions must include an identity,
and so $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_i(M) = \emptyset$ for $i > 2(n+m)+3(g-1)$.

$\mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ acts on $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_\bullet(M)$ levelwise by postcomposition -- non-parallel spheres are taken to non-parallel spheres under diffeomorphisms of~$M$.
We therefore get an action of $\mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ on $\|\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_\bullet(M)\|$ and since $\|\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_\bullet(M)\|$ is contractible, the homotopy orbit space of this action is a model for the classifying space:
\[
    B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M) \simeq \|\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_\bullet(M)\|/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}_F(M) \cong \|\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_\bullet /\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}_F(M) \|.
\]
Here we use that $(-)/\!\!/ G$ commutes with fat geometric realisation by \cref{lem:homotopy-orbits-functor}.
Since there are only simplices up to a certain dimension, it will suffice to prove that for all $n$ the space
\[
    \mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_n(M)/\!\!/\mathrm{Diff}_F(M)
\]
is homotopy finite. 
To reduce this to the case of $n=0$ recall from \cref{lem:face-map-is-finite-covering} that the last vertex map $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_n(M) \to \mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}(M)$ is a finite covering.
Therefore the map from $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel,\subset}_n(M) /\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ to $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}(M)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ is also a finite covering and it will suffice to show that the latter is homotopy finite.

By the homotopical orbit stabiliser theorem (\cref{lem:orbit-stabiliser-v2}) there is a decomposition 
    \[
        \mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}(M) /\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}_F(M)
        \simeq \coprod_{[x]} B\!\mathrm{Diff}_F(M,\Sigma)
    \]
    where the coproduct runs over a set of representatives of $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}(M)/\mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$. 
    Each of the terms in the coproduct is homotopy finite by  \cref{prop:finiteness-sphere-system}.
    Moreover, we showed $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}(M)/\mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ is finite in  \cref{lem:finitely-many-graphs-HM}.
    This completes the proof as we have written $\mathrm{Sep}^{\nparallel}(M)/\!\!/ \mathrm{Diff}_F(M)$ as a finite coproduct of homotopy finite spaces.

    Suppose we have a homotopy fiber sequence

        F \longrightarrow E \longrightarrow B

    Then $E$ is of finite type if \emph{and only if} $B$ is of finite type.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{cor:finite-type-tori-and-spheres}
    Let $M$ be a compact orientable $3$-manifold such that $\partial M$ is either empty or consists of spheres and incompressible tori.
    Then $B\!\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ is of finite type.
\begin{proof}
    The locally retractile action of $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ on $\mathrm{Emb}(D^3, \interior{M}) \simeq \mathrm{Fr}(M)$ yields via \cref{lem:orbit-stabiliser-transitive} the homotopy fiber sequence
    \[
        \mathrm{Fr}(M)' \longrightarrow B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{D^3}(M) \longrightarrow B\!\mathrm{Diff}(M)
    \]
    where $\mathrm{Fr}(M)' \subset \mathrm{Fr}(M)$ is an orbit of the action.
    Since $\mathrm{Fr}(M)' \subset \mathrm{Fr}(M)$ is a union of components it is homotopy finite.
    The total space $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_{D^3}(M)$ is homotopy finite by \cref{thm:more general Kontsevich-finiteness-conjecture}.
    It follows by \cref{lem:finite-type-fiberseq} that $B\!\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ is of finite type.
\end{proof}

Since Fr(M)' subset Fr(M) is a union of components it is homotopy finite. The total space B\!Diff_D^3(M) is homotopy finite by crefthm:more general Kontsevich-finiteness-conjecture. By work of Hatcher and Ivanov (see \cref{cor:Diff0-list}) we know that $\mathrm{Diff}_0(M) \simeq (S^1)^{\times b}$ for $b\in \{0,1,2\}$ and therefore $B\!\mathrm{Diff}_0(M) \simeq K(\mathbb{Z}^b, 2)$ is of finite type.
    Applying \cref{lem:finite-type-fiberseq} to the homotopy fiber sequence
    \[
        B\!\mathrm{Diff}_0(M) \longrightarrow B\!\mathrm{Diff}(M) \longrightarrow B(\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(M))
    \]
    we see that it suffices to check that $B(\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(M))$ is of finite type.
    By \cite[Theorem 7.1]{McCullough1991} the group $\pi_0\mathrm{Homeo}(M) \cong \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ is finitely presented and of type VFL.
    As pointed out in \cite[Theorem 1.1]{McCullough1991} this means that there is a finite index subgroup $\Gamma \le \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(M)$ such that $B\Gamma$ is homotopy finite 
    and therefore (e.g.~by \cref{lem:finite-type-fiberseq}) $B(\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(M))$ is of finite type.

nodes.statement: If M is disconnected, then we consider the finite index subgroup of those diffeomorphisms that do not permute components. This subgroup is a product of diffeomorphism groups of connected manifolds, so it will suffice to consider the case that M is connected. Moreover, we may assume M notcong S^1 times S^2, as this case is covered by crefcor:finite-type-tori-and-spheres. Since finite type spaces are also closed under homotopy pushouts and passing to finite covers, we can proceed as in the proof of crefthm:more general Kontsevich-finiteness-conjecture to reduce to the claim that for every separating system Sigma in Sep^nparallel(M) the space B\!Diff(M, Sigma) is of finite type. Here, instead of using crefcor:cut-along-spheres to cut along spheres, we use the homotopy fiber sequence \[ Diff'(Sigma) longrightarrow B\!Diff_Sigma(M) longrightarrow B\!Diff(M, Sigma) \] where Diff'(Sigma) subset Diff(Sigma) is the subgroup of those diffeomorphism of Sigma that extend to a diffeomorphism of M. The space Diff'(Sigma) is homotopy finite because Diff(S^2) simeq O(3) is, so by creflem:finite-type-fiberseq it will suffice to check that that B\!Diff_Sigma(M) is of finite type. nodes.statement: Let M = D^3 setminus (amalg_g interiorD^3) be obtained from the 3-disk by removing g smaller 3-disks on the first coordinate axis. Then there is a smooth SO(2)-action on M by rotating around that axis as indicated in creffig:rotation. The double M cup_partial M M of M is diffeomorphic to U_g, which therefore also has a smooth SO(2)-action, or equivalently a map SO(2) to Diff(U_g). The fixed points of this action are g+1 circles in U_g; we let S^1 subset U_g be one of them, and pick x_0 in S^1. Then we have group homomorphisms \[ SO(2) to Diff_S^1(U_g) to Diff_x_0(U_g) to GL_3^+ \] where the last map sends varphi in Diff_x_0(U_g) to its derivative d_x_0varphi. The composite map is the standard inclusion SO(2) to GL_3^+ and since the latter is equivalent to SO(3), the first claim follows after passing to classifying spaces. The second claim then follows since the map B\!SO(2) to B\!SO(3) induces the ring homomorphism on cohomology Q[p_1] longrightarrow Q[c_1] mapping the first Pontrjagin class p_1 to the square c_1^2 of the first Chern class. The required classes alpha are therefore the non-trivial image of Q[p_1] under the induced maps on cohomology.

Let $M = D^3 \setminus (\amalg_g \interior{D}^3)$ be obtained from the $3$-disk by removing $g$ smaller $3$-disks on the first coordinate axis.

    $\mathbb{Q}[p_1] \longrightarrow \mathbb{Q}[c_1]$
